utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I see that the appearances are the same as yesterday. That means Mr. Tieger and Mr. Waespi as the core team for the Prosecution. Mr. Misetic and Mr. Kehoe for Mr. Gotovina. I also see Mr. Akhavan. Mr. Akhavan, has the Chamber well understood that you might not be here on a daily basis as a member of the Defence team of Mr. Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: That remains to be clarified, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Akhavan. Then we have Mr. Kay, Mr. Cayley for Mr. Cermak, and we have Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Kuzmanovic for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For Mr. Cermak, Your Honour, we have additional counsel today, Ms. Higgins who is joining the Defence team who wasn't here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber was informed that Ms. Higgins joined the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest we now have on the record who is here that for the days to come and there will be many days to come, that if nothing is said about the appearances, that the Chamber expects Mr. Tieger, Mr. Waespi as being at least the core team, Mr. Misetic and Mr. Kehoe as the core team for Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Kay and Mr. Cayley to be present as the core Defence team of Mr. Cermak, and Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Kuzmanovic for Mr. Markac, that if any of these counsel is not present, that that will be put on the record at the beginning of each session. This is not to say that other members of Defence teams are not present, but if they speak, we'll see that on the record anyhow. Then we are about to start the trial against the three accused. In this case it is Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Cermak, and Mr. Markac. It is a case in which the parties will present their cases, at least the Prosecution to start, and if need be a Defence case, dealing with war crimes and crimes against humanity as charged in the indictment that allegedly have been committed during and in the aftermath of Operation Storm in the summer of 1995. Nine counts are brought against the accused. They are charged with individual responsibility, also in the form of a joint criminal enterprise in which they allegedly have participated together with others, and they're also held responsible by the Prosecution for command responsibility or superior responsibility depending on the positions. We'll be in court for this case for quite a long period of time. The Chamber expects and is confident that counsel will act as efficiently and professionally as possible, that we will not waste time on matters which are not really of importance for this case so that we can focus on what this Chamber wants to do during the month to come, that is to hear the evidence, the Prosecution evidence, whether Defence evidence, on this case, and the Chamber is confident that the parties will be able and they'll do their utmost best to assist the Chamber in the difficult determinations this Chamber will have to make in this case. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to give your opening statement in the case? I do understand that you'll be the one to start and that approximately at the natural time of a break Mr. Waespi will take over. That's then most likely after that break, and that you'll then after Mr. Waespi has given his portion of the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, learned colleagues for the Defence, this trial arises from the forcible elimination of Krajina Serbs from Croatia and the destruction of their community in August of 1995 and the roles and responsibilities of three men, generals in the Croatian army in that process. I'd like to show you first a map depicting Croatia and the territory of Croatia that was claimed by the Serbs and declared by them to be the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK. Your Honours, as you can see, it comprised essentially three parts, the first consisting of the large area at the left that you can see roughly from Knin in the south and up to the area of Vrgin Most, Petrinja in the north, the second part known as Western Slavonia which you see in the middle, and the third at the far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, at this moment whether I choose video, ELMO, or e-court, it's -- it now appears in e-court, but you started -- could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd be happy too. Your Honour, I had intended to show you initially this map which you now have on your screen. This map depicts Croatia and superimposed on it the boundaries of the area that was claimed by Croatian Serbs and declared by them to be the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK. And as I mentioned, it consists of three parts, the first to the left that I described a bit earlier, the portion in the middle known as Western Slavonia. That's that closest to a circular area. And then the portion at the far eastern end known as Eastern Slavonia. Now, I'll refer to the portion at the left for simplicity's sake as quite a number of witnesses will, as the Krajina generally, although that is not precisely a geographically accurate term. Your Honours, on the early morning of August 4th, 1995, Croatian soldiers began an attack to retake much of the Krajina, the portion to the left, back from the Krajina Serbs who had claimed it in 1991 and brutally cleansed it of virtually all Croats. Many among the Croatian soldiers had lost their homes and members of their families or friends as a result, and after years of failed negotiations were now coming back to reclaim their homes by force. This massive military operation which succeeded in retaking the area within a matter of days was known as Oluja, or Storm, Operation Storm. And although Operation Storm did not spell the end of the armed conflict between Serbs and Croats, it would mean the end for many Serbs of their lives on their ancestral lands. Your Honours, Croatia's right to reintegrate the Krajina into its internationally recognised borders is not in dispute here, but Operation Storm encompassed another objective as well, to drive out the Serb civilian population and ensure their permanent removal. By the time Operation Storm and its accompanying mop-up operations were over, almost the entire Serb population had been driven out and the Serb community was a scarred wasteland of destroyed villages and homes. By the end of the first day of the operation the vast majority of Krajina Serbs were in panic-stricken flight, not by accident but by design, through a successfully implemented plan to achieve just that through the shelling of civilian towns and villages. For the few who remained, largely the elderly and infirm, life became a nightmare during which their homes and villages were plundered and destroyed on a massive scale as they were arrested and harassed and as many were murdered. As one international observer wrote in anguish, "This is criminal. Is there nothing that can be done?" This case is about three men who were instrumental in those crimes, General Ante Gotovina was the commander of the Split Military District, and I'll show you that on the screen. That's the portion of this map that appears in red and in the chequered part of the red area. And he commanded approximately 30.000 troops in the area. General Gotovina planned and ordered the artillery operation that was intended to drive the Serb civilians out, and his troops engaged in widespread crimes against those Serbs who remained. General Mladen Markac was the commander of the special police, the military arm of the Ministry of Interior which worked in tandem with General Gotovina's forces and were also responsible for a portion of the artillery operation and responsible for the destruction that followed. And General Ivan Cermak who was sent personally by President Tudjman to assume the position of garrison commander and effectively the military governor of the area and who deflected international concerns about the crimes while failing to address them and facilitating their commission. These three men were not alone. Foremost among their co-participants in this joint effort to force Serbs from the Krajina was President Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia and the Supreme Commander of it's armed forces, as well as other high-ranking officials. The contribution of the three accused to this joint effort, however, will be the focus of this trial. Your Honours, although this case is about the crimes that occurred from the beginning of August to the end of September 1995, it may be helpful to put them briefly in context and recognising in so doing that no summary can capture the many complexities and many tragedies of ethnic conflict. The Serbs of the Krajina had lived there for centuries. The name Krajina itself refers back to the military empire established by the Habsburg Empire in the 16th Century to resist Ottoman incursions during which time many Serbs came to the region. While there are some who may trace the roots of the conflict between Serbs and Croats back through the centuries, you will hear relatively little dating back that far. You will, however, hear about the conflict's links to the events of the more recent past and particularly to events during World War II. During that time, the violently nationalist Ustasha regime murdered Serbs on a massive scale. The precise numbers to this day remain a subject of controversy in the region but even the most conservative estimates capture the appalling and systematic nature of the crimes committed against Serbs during that time. At the same time, the Serbian Chetnik forces garnered a reputation among Croats for brutality, and in the conflict that followed the disintegration of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, Serbs and Croats routinely referred to each other pejoratively and often themselves proudly as Ustashas or Chetniks. As the dissolution of Yugoslavia began to become a reality in the early '90s, nationalist parties emerged to represent and promote the perceived interests of each group. In Croatia where Serbs constituted 12 to 13 per cent of the population at the time, the Croatian nationalist party HDZ, standing for Croatian Democratic Union, won the 1990 elections under the leadership of Franjo Tudjman. The HDZ sought an independent Croatia, the realisation of a long-held dream to restore a fully independent Croatian nation. Although the Serbian nationalist party SDS, standing for Serbian Democratic Party, was not a particularly successful party in those elections, it began to gather greater support among Serbs in the face of evolving events, which included a new draft constitution that removed the status of Serbs as a constituent nation in Croatia and imposed reduction of Serbs from the police and generally increasing inter-ethnic tensions and violence. Now, this is not to suggest that the actions of the SDS were simply reactive or justified, but it does, however, reflect the synergy of nationalism at the time as Serbs became more nationalistic and Croatian nationalists gathered further support in the face of growing Serb nationalism in a vicious and tragic spiral. The SDS under the leadership of first Milan Babic and then Milan Martic took the position that if Croatia could leave Yugoslavia in which Serbs were a constituent nation, then the Serbs in Croatia could leave Croatia with the land they considered to be theirs. Working closely with Slobodan Milosevic they initiated steps to separate and control areas they deemed Serbian in anticipation of linking those areas to Serbia and to territories in Bosnia claimed by the Bosnian Serbs. The Croatian Serb leaders first declared autonomous regions, the outlines of which you saw on the screen earlier, and then a state, the RSK. The RSK encompassed areas such as those around Knin, which will be the subject of discussion during the course of this case where Serbs were the majority, and it also encompassed areas such as Eastern Slavonia where the population was more mixed or where Croats were the majority. In the course of or after taking these territories, RSK forces often assisted by the Yugoslav Army or other forces from Belgrade, forcibly expelled Croats through murder, inhumane acts and other crimes. These crimes formed the basis for the prosecutions and convictions before this very Tribunal of Serbian leaders Babic and Martic. By the beginning of 1992, after the Serbs had taken approximately one-third of Croatian territory, the international community brokered a cease-fire and the introduction of UN troops to monitor and maintain the peace. Four United Nations Protected Areas or UNPAs were declared and created, and you see those on the screen, and UN peacekeeping forces were introduced. This area on screen now is the area covered by this indictment and was part of one of those protected areas known as Sector South. Between January 1992 when the UNPAs were created and the beginning of August 1995, the international community attempted to resolve of the crisis through various peace proposals or peace plans. These efforts attempted to balance Croatia's insistence on the integrity of its internationally recognised borders, an objective shared by the international community, with the Serbian insistence on an independent state within the territory you've seen. The best known of those efforts the Z-4 plan, offered the Krajina Serb leadership substantial autonomy within Croatia but the RSK leadership and particularly Milan Martic rebuffed these efforts. For Croats this enhanced the risk of a long-term stalemate that could eventually make the RSK a fait accompli. And as these ultimately fruitless negotiations went on, Croatia was in the process of transforming its initially modest fighting forces into a formidable and well-equipped army. Between 1992 and 1995, it tested its capabilities in several military operations into the Serb-held territory. These included Miljevacki plateau, Maslenica bridge, Medak Pocket, and Operation Flash, about which you'll hear. Now, Your Honours, while the conduct of these operations is not directly in dispute in this case or at issue in this case, you will hear evidence that they gave rise to international concern over the treatment of Serb civilians and that Serbs in the Krajina understood that civilians had not always faired well at the hands of the Croatian army. In July 1995, a combination of factors converged - most memorably the Srebrenica massacre and the threat to Bihac by Serbian forces - factors that persuaded President Tudjman that Croatia would have sufficient international support or at least would not suffer any political repercussions for retaking the Krajina through military force. The first step toward this objective was known as Operation Summer during which General Gotovina's forces took Glamoc and Grahovo in Bosnia and you see them depicted here on the map. In so doing they captured the high ground above Knin, which was the capital of the RSK, thus bringing it within direct observation and within artillery range and simultaneously cutting Knin off from its lifeline to Belgrade with its value as a supply centre for Serb forces. Meanwhile, Croatian forces under General Gotovina's command regularly shelled Serb villages and farms in the Krajina increasing Serb fears and triggering a flow of Serb refugees into Knin. On July 31, 1995, in a meeting that was captured on tape as were many others, President Tudjman met with his key military and political advisors, including General Gotovina and General Markac, to plan the attack on Krajina Serbs for which Operation Summer had set the stage. President Tudjman expressed the goal in this way: "In which way do we resolve it? That is the subject of our discussion today. We have to inflict such blows that the Serbs will to all practical purposes disappear, that is to say, the areas we do not take at once must capitulate within a few days. Therefore, our main task is not Bihac but to inflict such blows in several directions that the Serbian forces will no longer be able to recover but will have to capitulate." To strike such blows that the Serbs will to all practical purposes disappear, to inflict such blows that the Serbian forces will no longer be able to recover. These words may appear somewhat ambiguous initially but as the discussion continues, it becomes clear what President Tudjman has in mind. After hearing the operational recommendations of his top military figures and insisting that the Serb forces not be encircled but given a way out so that last-ditch stand which would cost Croatian casualties could be averted, President Tudjman observed that something was missing. It was time, he said, to hit Knin, which had remained untouched while Croatian towns and villages had been destroyed. "Gentlemen, I accept your views in principle. There is still something missing, and that is the fact that in such a situation when we undertake a general offensive in the entire area, even greater panic will break out in Knin than has to date. Accordingly, we should provide for certain forces which will be directly engaged in the direction of Knin. And, particularly, gentlemen, please remember how many Croatian villages and towns have been destroyed, but that's still not the situation in Knin today ..." He goes on: "But their counter-attack from Knin and so forth, it would provide a very good justification for this action and accordingly, we have the pretext to strike if we can with artillery you can ... for complete demoralisation." General Gotovina immediately assured President Tudjman that this represented no problem. "Mr. President, at this time we completely control Knin with our hardware. That's not a problem. If there is an order to strike at Knin, we will destroy it in its entirety in a few hours. With armoured forces, and medium and long-range missile systems." President Tudjman emphasised again that the time to pay back the Serbs had arrived. "Therefore, we need to be bold. That means not just having things under control but taking it back as quickly as possible so he gets a taste of it and we pay him back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you included the word "back" which I do not find on my screen, the first "back." Take it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then President Tudjman made crystal clear what was to happen when they strike Knin with artillery for complete demoralisation: "We've said it here, that they should be given a way out here ... because it is important that those civilians set out, and then the army will follow them, and when the columns set out, they will have a psychological impact on each other." General Gotovina immediately underscored President Tudjman's point. He noted that civilians were already leaving Knin and said: "That means that if we continue this pressure, probably for some time to come there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay who have no possibility of leaving." President Tudjman was concerned about one problem that could have international ramifications. Was the attack on Knin possible without hitting the UNCRO camp which was located on the southern edge of Knin? General Gotovina assured him that there was no reason for concern. And first I'd like to show Your Honour the map of Knin, and this depicts here at the southern portion the UNCRO facility that President Tudjman was speaking about when he expressed his concern about whether that would be hit. And if we could return to the large picture. Just so you can place it in the context of Knin. As I said, Your Honour, after President Tudjman posed this question, General Gotovina responded assuring him at that there was no reason for concern. "At this moment, we can engage in extremely precise operations at Knin, systematically, without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located. (We have all the photographs and know exactly ...)." And he said a moment later: "This moment all of our weapons are guided, directly guided." The intention to get Serb civilians to flee was also reflected in efforts to broadcast false radio messages and drop fake leaflets that pretended to be from Serb authorities, leaflets and broadcasts instructing civilians to flee. Here's one of them instructing the entire civilian population to withdraw from the area and providing a route because of the expected attack by the "Ustasha army." This was not perfectly done as you'll see from the stamp at the bottom. The first four letters are in Latin script instead of Cyrillic. But that's not the only reason you know about these efforts. The minister of defence later bragged about them and General Gotovina himself later wrote in his book, which was entitled "Offences and operations of the Croatian army and the Croatian Defence Council," which was published in 1996, in referring to leaflets for the population to leave he wrote that: "It is true that such leaflets were dropped from aircraft prior to Operation Oluja and that this action had an effect." Indeed General Gotovina was sufficiently impressed that he used it in his next operation, that time in Bosnia and that time purporting to be from the Bosnian Serb army, again directing the Serb civilian population to leave. These efforts were also accompanied by a broadcast from President Tudjman ostensibly urging Serbs to stay. I'd like to read out President Tudjman's -- well, I think you'll actually see it in Sanction, but I'd like you to be to able to hear the actual language spoken by -- or words spoken by President Tudjman, and particularly the end of his words and the little chuckle at the end which reflect, we submit, his characterisation of this effort. If that could be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this is not in evidence at this moment. Therefore, it might not be a major problem. There's no translation. But just for guidance to the parties if any video or audio is played, sufficient time should be given even if we see the English text on our screens it should be on the official transcript as well. Therefore, I will work out at a later stage a procedure by which we have both the words spoken on the English and on the French transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to read it out at this point if that would be helpful and put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could read it out briefly so that it then also will appear on the French transcript which is produced a couple of days later. Please proceed first by reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What President Tudjman said is this: "A leaflet of this sort, general chaos, the victory of the Croatian army supported by the international community and so forth, Serbs, you are already withdrawing and so forth and we are appealing to you not to withdraw. We guarantee. This means giving them a way out while pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera." "While pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera," with the knowing chuckle at the end. These broadcasts complemented the effort through shelling, leaflets, and fake broadcasts to get the civilians to flee while simultaneously providing a fig leaf for Croatian efforts and intentions. Your Honours, the departure of the Serbs realised a long-term political ambition of President Tudjman who had long believed, like other nationalist leaders in the region, that multi-ethnic states were unsustainable, that relatively large numbers of people of another ethnicity threatened the stability of the state. This was a position he openly expressed to international diplomats or to other nationalist leaders in the region. Put more starkly as one of President Tudjman's aides said to the UN ambassador, Serbs in the Krajina were viewed as a cancer on the stomach of Croatia. And the solution to this problem was reconfiguring the demographics of Croatia. In 1992 he discussed the division in Bosnia between its Serb, Croat and Muslim ethnic groups through population transfers with Bosnian Serb leader Nikola Koljevic, another proponent resolving the crisis in Yugoslavia through largely homogenous states built along ethnic lines. As Koljevic said: "The term 'homogeneity' was, as you know, vilified in Yugoslavia. Why should it be something terrible for people to live with people who are closest to them?" And President Tudjman agreed: "Wherever national problems so conceived emerged as they did with us, that was resolved from World War I and World War II. That was brought to a conclusion by exchanges." As one of President Tudjman's advisors related in August 1995 about a conversation he had with Slobodan Milosevic: "If there are fewer Serbs in Croatia and Croats in Serbia, I have to tell you the better our future relations are going to be." Referring to Eastern Slavonia, the sole remaining territory under the control of the Croatian Serbs, he noted: "An autonomous region within the Republic of Croatia would be a potential Trojan horse for Serbian politics." Indeed, Your Honours, as the evidence will show, the preoccupation with the risk of a continuing Serb presence in Croatia was even reflected in President Tudjman's rejection of peace -- of possible peace agreements that would provide the land to Croatia but which ran the risk that in so doing large numbers of Serbs would return to Croatia. Instead of accepting an agreement that would give land back to Croatia, he preferred to put Croats from those rejected areas into areas such as Western Slavonia that no longer contained Serbs, thereby keeping a largely homogenous state and Western Slavonia was now available for such a purpose. As one of President Tudjman's advisors said to him after Operation Flash during which the Croatian army retook Western Slavonia: "The Serb problem in Western Slavonia has been solved. There's no more than a thousand of them including old women and the elderly, and there are no more than 300 to 400 people who are political factors." And after Serbs had been driven from the Krajina, the same goal of a reduced Serb presence meant keeping them out. I'll quote from a conversation about one part of Krajina where Serbs had lived. "If you ask me the first, I define five priorities according to the urgency of colonising these places with Croats. If you ask me, this thing right here is the first and second priority. We should bring Croats back here urgently and this area should be urgently colonised with Croats and we should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again. Because, that's where we were cut off." President Tudjman was more emphatic: "Not even 10 per cent." Now, this reference to colonisation of Croats reflected a related preoccupation of President Tudjman to ensure that areas emptied of Serbs were quickly refilled with Croats. In the context of Knin and other cities that had been overwhelmingly Serb before the war but had long ago been Croat, that meant, as he said on the 23rd of August, we should make Knin Croatian as fast as possible. This was achieved in two ways, through the destruction of their community which sent an unmistakable signal to Serbs that they shouldn't or couldn't come back and through bureaucratic obstacles to keep them out. First President Tudjman imposed laws to restrict the time within which Serbs could reclaim their property, the property they had abandoned when they were driven out of the Krajina. Quoting President Tudjman: "I am with the more radical, if someone has left the country and does not appear there, I don't know, a month or three months, et cetera, that shall be considered, think of the wording, state property, et cetera. We have come out of a war, et cetera, define it like that." And then the comment: "Not three months. Three months is too long because we ..." And President Tudjman again: "Okay. A month then." This initially imposed period of 30 days was expanded to a largely symbolic 90 days under international pressure, although even that period was also recognised by the international community as accomplishing what Croatian authorities had in mind, and that is an effective barrier to Serb return. At the same time that President Tudjman and Croatian authorities imposed these purposefully restricted time limits, they also intentionally created obstacles to ensure that Serbs could not return in time. Thus in response to questions about entry visas for Serbs who wanted to come back, President Tudjman said in August 1995: "I would not give anything. You have to give instructions to the customs that they should not let people with papers to cross the border."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard you say "with papers" but it reads "without papers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Thanks for the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then the comment: "President, let us get inspired the way it is in Western Slavonia." And that's a quote and let me mention that that was the area that was the subject of Operation Flash that we mentioned earlier and the subject of the earlier reference to the problem being solved because there were few Serbs left. "It was very positive for us because no one came back." Adding then: "We should not let them come back -- we should not let them come here. No way." And as President Tudjman further explained later in the same discussion: "If we let 204 persons come here, tomorrow you would have 1.204, and in 10 days 12.000. Nothing for now." The combination of these purposefully restricted time periods and the obstacles to return was quite effective as stated in a Security Council report on the 31st of December, 1995, given the various barriers in crossing the border, requiring the Serbs to return within that time frame to reclaim their property constitutes -- "Constitutes a virtually insurmountable obstacle." Following the successful effort to drive Serbs out, President Tudjman spoke with great satisfaction with the new circumstances. In a speech on the 26th of August, 1995, to cheering crowds he stressed Knin's importance as a "royal Croatian town," which never again will anyone be able to endanger."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour if the Court would prefer we can play that again and I can read it out for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could already try to do it in the way in which I intend to do it during trial, that is that especially if the words are spoken very quickly, which seems not to be very much the case here, but that if then -- but if there are any other suggestions by the interpreters, I'd like to hear that one the interpreters reads whether the English text as it appears on the screen reflects what is -- correctly reflects what is said in the original language and that the other interpreter then reads this text aloud so that it appears on the English channel and that it also appears on the transcript. For the French interpreters, then one of the interpreters, and I know it's teamwork but it works out well usually, that the one interpreter reads whether the English, as we see it on the screen, correctly reflects what is said in the original language, and that the other interpreter who might not be able to follow the speed of speech then translates -- translates it into French so that we have it on the French audio, which will finally result in a French transcript. That is my suggestion. I know it's a problem. Could we give that a test at this very moment and see whether it works? If there's any comment from the -- either the English or the French booth. I'd like to hear it. I'm at this moment listening to Channel 4, the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From the English booth we will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] Thank you. Then could you please replay it, Mr. Tieger, and we'll check whether it appears on both the English and the French audio channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] But today it is Croatian Knin and never again will it go back to what was before, when they spread cancer which has been destroying the Croatian national being in the middle of Croatia and didn't allow the Croatian people to be truly alone on its own, that Croatia becomes capable of being independent -- an independent and sovereign state, a part of the world community of sovereign states under the heaven."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to thank the interpreters. I wished that all audios and videos would contain speech at such a slow speed, which would certainly help us, but it seems to work well. Thank you for your cooperation. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As President Tudjman said a year later in a speech on the first anniversary of taking Knin and referring to an ancient king: "We have returned Zvonimir's city, the Croatian city of Knin, to the lap of the Croatian motherland clean as it was in Zvonimir's time." All of these factors, Your Honours, reflect the intent behind the discussion of the 31st of July about taking the opportunity, the pretext to strike with artillery for complete demoralisation. And in accordance with the discussion between President Tudjman and Generals Gotovina and Markac, here is the order given by General Gotovina to do precisely what President Tudjman had stated. To shell Knin and other relatively large towns of the Krajina and one across the border. "These are the tasks of the artillery-rocket groups." As you can see the order instructs them to engage in a number of conventional uses of artillery, provide support to main forces by launching a powerful assault on the enemy's first line, hit the enemy's command posts, his communication centres, his artillery positions, and, Your Honours, in addition to that, by targeting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac with artillery fire. This specific identification of whole towns as a target alongside of military targets was echoed in the orders of his subordinates. I'd like to show you the order from his artillery commander. As you can see toward the bottom of the screen, that order provides: "Neutralise the artillery positions of enemy batteries, destroy the enemy's communications centres and command post. During the attack, secure the flanks with units from the 1st echelon." And then: "Shell the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac." And as that flow continued here's an artillery attachment for one of the four operational groups, that is Operational Group Zadar and the task for an artillery rocket group. We'll go to the next page. Again a number of conventional uses of artillery. Neutralise the enemy artillery battery positions and destroy their communications centres, command post. Secure the 1st echelon, combat echelon unit, flanks in attack. And again, alongside of these military or conventional military objectives, "Put the following towns under artillery fire: Benkovac, Obrovac and Gracac." Thus beyond a legitimate effort to reintegrate the Krajina through military means, these orders reflect the plan discussed on July 31st to drive Serb civilians out by shelling and thereby realising the ambition of a mainly homogenous state that was largely free of Serbs. Now, Your Honours, you will hear evidence of the shelling of other towns and villages in the Krajina, indeed more than a hundred were targeted where there was no meaningful military function or purpose, but as General Gotovina stated in his book, Knin was the most important target. Your Honours, there are a few photographs of Knin on the screen. Although Knin was not a large city by many standards, perhaps 15.000 people, it was nevertheless as you've heard a place of significance to both Serbs and Croats. To the Croats it was the ancient capital and town of Croatian kings and now the centre and symbol of Serbian separatism. For Serbs in the Krajina, it was their capital and principal city, but for those who lived there, it was their home where their families had lived for generations, where families lived, children went to school, where there were playgrounds, bakeries, shops. In addition to the Serbian population in Knin there was a considerable number of members of the international community. As you've heard already, UNCRO was there. That's the United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation which succeeded UNPROFOR. As well as representatives of the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM, United Nations Civilian Police, UNCIVPOL; United Nations Military Observers, UNMOs; and others, many of whom you will be hearing from during the course of this case. These internationals represented the peace forces assembled by the international community to monitor and maintain the increasingly precarious cease-fire back in July and the beginning of August 1995. Many of them not surprisingly had military experience and a number of them from whom you'll hear had an artillery background. Although people in Knin were aware of Croatian military moves and the risk of conflict and some people had left, the vast majority had remained. Indeed, in the days preceding Storm, Knin's population had swelled and increased from the arrival of Serb refugees who had fled from the areas being shelled by Croatian forces under General Gotovina's control. Knin was hardly a military stronghold as you'll hear and the Croatian army, which had impressive intelligence capabilities was well aware of the lack of defence and military capability within Knin and the single unsupported line of defence along the zone of separation. In Knin there were no trenches dug, no fortifications constructed, no anti-mines laid, no troop positions, and not a single air-raid or defence drill. There were almost no troops in the town since virtually all the troops were at the front lines in preparation for the imminent attack. As I mentioned, the entire Serbian army defence consisted of a single perimeter that lacked second and third lines, in case the front line was penetrated. Now you'll see on screen an aerial photo of Knin, Your Honours, and as you can see although it's very small, Knin held a number of sites with varying degrees of military significance. The military headquarters, the parliament, the police headquarters, the barracks, the petroleum and oil depot, the railway yard, a factory that made screws. But in any event, General Gotovina's interest was not in the military advantage to be gained by destroying, capturing, or neutralising any of these specific sites but in doing what had been planned, demoralising the civilians and getting them to flee. And as you will hear, the shelling of Knin was achieved in a manner to achieve precisely that purpose and virtually everyone who experienced it recognised it as an attack on the town as a whole and its civilian inhabitants. At precisely 5.00 a.m. on the 4th of August, 1995, the attack began with a massive rocket and artillery barrage which stunned the population, most of whom were settled in their homes. Indeed, some observers from whom you'll hear were reminded of World War II documentary footage or of the shelling of Sarajevo. In any event, all were stunned by its ferocity. Shells fell in all parts of the town, in areas where there was a mix of military sites and civilian structures and in purely residential areas. The one place shells didn't fall as General Gotovina had assured President Tudjman was on the UNCRO headquarters, underscoring the capacity to control and direct fire. As this went on, many people huddled in basements in terror awaiting a letup in shelling so that they could figure out what to do and where to go. At UNCRO headquarters, UNCRO officials observed the shelling quickly realising that although the shells were landing all over the city, their headquarters were being purposefully spared. When UNCRO members left the compound to rescue some of their personnel and civilian employees who were outside, they found themselves under fire even when in purely residential areas and observed residential areas being shelled. And UNCRO received reports from outposts around the Krajina that civilian population centres were being indiscriminately shelled.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The UNCRO commander General Forand, attempted to stop the shelling of civilians and civilian areas by sending the following protest now on your screen to General Gotovina. This is to protest in the most vigorous manner the unprovoked artillery attack on Knin on the towns of Drnis, Medak, Bunic, Benkovac, and Kistanje. Numerous civilian casualties have been caused as well as extensive material damage. "I demand the cessation of these attacks immediately --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, when you read it's well known that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you speed up, and since you have been asked to speak -- to slow down, could you please resume reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "In my opinion, this aggression against unarmed civilians is completely contrary to international humanitarian law and I will document all attacks fully for investigation by international authorities." The message was given to a military observer to deliver to the Croatian army liaison officer who reported -- and the UNMO reported back to General Forand that had been delivered. The intense barrage continued for approximately two hours or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the French translation -- please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The intense barrage which had commenced at 5.00 a.m. continued for approximately two hours or so until subsiding into sporadic harassment fire which lasted for the remainder of the 4th, indeed until well into the late hours. While estimates of the precise number of shells that fell during the bombardment vary, there is no dispute among the witnesses that during the initial barrage and the subsequent sporadic shelling hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of shells and rockets, up to much larger estimates, were fired into Knin. By the night of the 4th a panicky flight from Knin was underway. This excerpt from the operational diary of the Split military district shows that the army and General Gotovina were well aware of this: "Panic in Knin, evacuation of civilians and Krajina Corps command, that is KK command, expected. ED will follow up on that as well as observation posts. Their in-depth communications are broken. They have no reserves." Your Honours, this panic-stricken flight that I referred to and it's referred to in this document was visible that evening and on the morning of the 5th. Yet despite the awareness that the military was in flight, the following morning the pattern was repeated. At approximately 05.20 that morning on August 5th, another massive artillery barrage was unleashed on Knin, followed again by sporadic shelling. Again the shelling spanned the city, landing in areas all around. By 10.00 the Croatian army entered, not in anticipation of a street battle but convoy style, in triumph to a largely deserted city. Although we will never know the precise number of people who were killed by the shelling or injured which by the shelling in Knin or Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and the other towns and villages that were shelled. Witnesses on the spot contemporaneously observed bodies of those killed by shelling in the streets of Knin and in the Knin hospital. Estimating from those observations some 20 to 30 or more. This is quite consistent with the report from head of UN peacekeeping operations Akashi to then under-secretary General Kofi Annan on the 23rd of August when he reported seeing four large mounds that gave the impression of a mass grave and where Croatian officials noted that the bodies had been placed in bags ten centimetres apart. A Croatian Civil Defence official present at the site told Akashi that most of the deceased were civilians from Knin who had been killed during the Croatian shelling of the city on the 4th and 5th of August. There were 96 crosses at that time marking the mass grave site. Your Honours, there are several principles that govern the lawfulness of shelling. Foremost among them are the principles of distinction and proportionality. Thus with respect to distinction, targeting of civilians or civilian objects is impermissible, and in keeping with that principle of distinction between military and civilian targets, shelling that does not discriminate between civilian and military targets is impermissible whether it results from shelling that is not directed at a specific military target or shelling that uses a method of a nature to strike military objects or civilians without distinction. And assuming compliance with these principles of distinction, proportionality requires the expected civilian death, injury or damage not to be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. As I mentioned earlier, virtually all of those who experienced the shelling understood that it was directed toward the civilian population. Some understood it because the shells landed on their houses or in their neighbourhoods. Others because they saw from a safer vantage that shells were falling in purely residential areas or were being fired randomly around the town. Some with a military background or knowledge of artillery recognised some of the weapon systems used including rockets used for area use rather than pinpointing particular targets or recognised targeting procedures being employed including adjusting fire to hit more precisely within residential areas. At other times there were no such adjustments. Shells were lobbed in individually so that they would fall relatively randomly without honing in on a particular target and with little likelihood of destroying a specific target. All observed on the second morning the intense shelling of the city from which the military had fled. The manner in which the shelling was conducted, Your Honours, reflects both its departure from the permissible uses of artillery as well as the intention behind it. To shell towns as a whole, to frighten civilians into flight. Croatian officials downplayed the attack reflecting their awareness of its purpose and illegality. On the 7th of August, the minister of defence said in a press conference: "We have tried everything to treat civilians according to the international law. When we began the action on the first day we tried to avoid all large settlements thugs giving the Serbs another chance to surrender. However, when they began shelling Croatian cities on the free territory instead, we decided to carry out the operation of capturing all these settlements to and end." General Gotovina's lengthy account of the operation in his book omits the artillery attack on the 4th entirely. Rather than avoiding attacks on large settlements on humanitarian grounds as suggested by the minister of defence, the shelling of Knin and other towns was at the core of the plan to drive Serbs out. Here are two additional documents, reports from an artillery unit commander on the 4th of August reflecting in part its execution. On the 1st we see highlighted at 6.30 hours five projectiles from a T-130-millimetre at the hospital in Knin. And at 8.00, six projectiles from a T-130-millimetre at a residential area in Knin. And in the second report we see at 13.30 hours, firing with eight projectiles from a T-130-millimetre at Knin. And at 15.00 hours in irregular intervals, a total of 18 projectiles fired from a T-130-millimetre at the general area of Knin. Despite the bombardment, Your Honour, the Court should not get the wrong impression. This was not Stalingrad or Vukovar where weeks of shelling reduced the city to rubble. It was not the most destructive shelling of the war. But that is precisely the point. The intention was not to destroy Knin, the city of Zvonimir into which President Tudjman intended to resettle Croats but to drive out Serbs. You will hear evidence during the course of this case of a provisional assessment of damage in Knin that was undertaken by UNMOs on the 17th of August which found that 44 buildings were damaged, 21 severely and 23 slightly, and that they were in the close vicinity of military targets. And you'll also learn that those who actually conducted this provisional assessment at the time emphasised its cursory nature and later conducted patrols that identified further damage and shell craters in purely residential areas where there were no possible military targets. The subsequent findings are consistent with the amount of destruction noted by other witnesses and also with a final document on destruction entitled "Data on population left and destroyed houses," which indicates hundreds of houses destroyed or partially destroyed in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the benefit of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Other witnesses, Your Honour, also observed that as time went on they were able to identify additional evidence of shelling in purely residential areas. Indeed even taking the provisional assessment on its face which reflects more than 40 civilian buildings, including large apartment buildings in which many people resided had been damaged by the shelling, when buildings such as the military headquarters, clearly a military target, was struck by one or two shells and left basically intact, these -- these factors indicate damage to civilian buildings at a level in comparison to the damage to significant military targets, which indicates the indiscriminate nature of the shelling. Your Honours, the Court will also hear evidence of an order to evacuate by Milan Martic, the president of the RSK and also of a pre-existing evacuation plan. Now, here is that plan which as you can see was issued approximately 12 hours after the shelling of Knin and other towns and villages had commenced. The facts of the evacuation plan in the evacuation order are these: The evacuation plan represented the customary efforts of civilian bodies, civilian protection bodies, common to most states. There was a civilian defence section of the RSK government that had prepared an evacuation plan in the event of various forms of emergency, including not only shelling of civilian areas but also other emergencies such as natural disasters. It contemplated the temporary removal of people at risk to safer areas, generally into larger towns, but with the larger towns under fire, they had to move farther as the Martic order itself reflects. Martic issued the order after a full day of shelling and after people were already starting to fleeing in panic. Their panic was reflected in the conditions of their homes after they were gone, with food left on the table and personal effects left behind, and by a meeting that UNCRO officials had with RSK officials who had sought their help and during which it became clear that nothing had been prepared. As President Tudjman would say to a crowd a few weeks later: "They didn't have time to collect neither their dirty money, foreign currency, or their underwear." Most importantly, Your Honours, President Tudjman, General Gotovina, and General Markac were not content to rely on Serbian fears or an official evacuation order to rid Knin and the Krajina of Serbs. They shelled and dropped fake leaflets and broadcast false messages in order to get the civilian population to flee many hours before the evacuation order was issued in response. The order certainly did not affect the purpose and nature of shelling which was intended to drive the civilians out and executed well before he issued the order. Thus as reported by the HV head of intelligence about the events of the 4th: "The majority of towns, (Knin, Drnis, Gracac, Plaski, Petrinja, Dubica) were directly threatened, which caused a large-scale (organised or spontaneous) moving out of civilians and also an organised moving out of the highest state organs (moving out of the government to the area of BiH, most probably to the area between Drvar and Sipovo) and the abandonment of military facilities ..." As President Tudjman said on the 26th of August during a triumphal trip through the Krajina: "Owing to the strength of the Croatian army, the wisdom of our decisions and our leadership, they disappeared in two to three days." It was indeed the decisions that the political and military leadership had taken and their execution by the army that led to the disappearance of most of the Serbian community from the Krajina. Your Honours, you previously foreshadowed the bifurcation in the opening address. This would be the point at which Mr. Waespi would commence, so it may be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. We will have a break -- how much time would Mr. Waespi need approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think approximately 50 minutes to an hour, if I have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifty minutes to an hour. Then we will have a break for half an hour and we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to make two remarks on the matter we dealt with before the break, that is how to get the text of video and audio clips correctly on the transcript. First of all, I would like to emphasise that although the assistance of the interpreters to see whether the written text reflects what is in the original is highly appreciated, at the same time it's not their task, and it's not their responsibility that this is a correct interpretation. So therefore, we do appreciate if the interpreters would inform us about any striking difference between -- they notice between the text originally spoken and they see on the written text. Therefore, again it is assisting us in achieving the best result, but it's something extra and not within their task and not within their responsibility. Nevertheless, if they find anything that makes clear that the translation does not reflect, I'm not talking about half a word but really important differences, that's highly appreciated if they will draw our attention to that. Second is that working on the basis of the written text on the bottom of the screen is not very easy to do. Therefore, the parties should provide, and I see that the first steps may have been taken already, that they should provide the booth with hard copies of at least the English text but preferably also the original text so that the interpreters, if they're doing this extra work, that they don't have to work from just four, five or six lines on the bottom of their screens which is very difficult to do. So therefore the parties should provide the booth with hard copies of transcripts, preferably in two languages; if that's not possible, at least in the original language. Then apart from that what further is reflected on the transcript, what appears in the transcript is a matter the Chamber would like to be in charge of in every respect. That means even where we encourage a good and informal [Realtime transcript read in error "formal"] relationship with all those who are assisting us and the parties, that finally anything that should be verified on whether something appears or will appear is primarily the responsibility of registry and the Chamber; and therefore any such contacts which would have any impact on what we finally find in the transcript, it's appreciated if the Chamber, as was done today, is informed about such contacts. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. As my colleague Alan Tieger announced, let me address in more detail the crimes which the Prosecution says the accused are responsible. Before I do that I would like to give you a brief snapshot of the main aspect of the military offensive Operation Storm and I will use a couple of the maps from this court binder which we have given to Your Honours, members of the Defence, the registry a couple of days earlier, but we will use these maps on the screen as well. Your Honours, the breadth of Operation Oluja or Storm extends beyond the scope of the indictment. Whilst the indictment focuses on the areas of responsibility of the three accused, Operation Storm was conducted over territory extending beyond the geographical limits relative to the indictment and involved the participation of an overall force of 127.000 members of the Croatian forces including military police and approximately 2.500 members of the Ministry of Interior, the MUP. Map 15, Your Honours, in your court binder is a map that depicts the whole spectrum of Operation Storm. The focus of the indictment is the southern portion of the Krajina where the forces subordinated to the three accused were deployed, predominantly the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. The manpower of the Split Military District for Operation Storm, as Mr. Tieger already said, amounted to approximately 30.000, including 10.000 newly mobilised troops. On map 15, if we can focus now on the southern part of map 15, you see the line-up of the Croatian forces involved in Operation Storm. Grouped clockwise, shown in yellow, starting with the 4th Guards Brigade and ending at the other side of the spectrum with the Special Police commanded by the Accused Markac. These are all the units, Your Honours, listed in annex A of the indictment. On the same map you can see the defending forces, the RSK forces, shown in red, mainly consisting of units of the 7th Dalmatian Corps organised mainly in brigades. Already in looking at this map, Your Honours, you can see how SVK, the army of the RSK was already in a pocket with the Croatian forces surrounding them at the beginning of Operation Storm. You heard a number of times, Your Honours, that Operation Storm commenced on the 4th of August, 1995, in the early morning hours with air and artillery support. The majority of towns including Knin, you know where it is, Drnis, Benkovac, and Gracac were directly attacked with artillery. In his book the Accused Gotovina, the book has been cited before, "Offensive Battles and Operations of the HV and HVO," wrote and I quote: "Towns of Knin and Drvar were shelled from the firing positions in the Bosansko Grahovo area." The arrow to the right. "With 430-millimetre calibre cannons. Knin was also targeted from the Miljevci area," second arrow, "with the same calibre cannons. Gracac was shelled from the firing positions in the Rovanjska area. And lastly, Benkovac was targeted from the firing positions in the area of Mount Debeljak." By nightfall of the 4th of August, the SVK and RSK leadership were in disarray. Panic reigned in Knin and inhabitants left in masses. Thus the stage was set for the HV to enter Knin the following day. Next day, already by the 5th of August, SVK had ceased to function following the break-up of its command and communication systems. On the 5th of August, as you already heard, HV units mainly the 7th Guards Brigade and other units of the 4th Guards Brigade entered Knin, seized the town, and around by midday the Croatian state flag was hoisted at the fortress in Knin. In addition, Your Honours, to the seizure of Knin by the end of 5th August, 1995, the Split Military District controlled, according to General Gotovina's own assessment, 70 per cent of the northern Dalmatia area which had until then been under ASK control. The next couple of days, Your Honours, Croatian forces including the Special Police took control over towns such as, and I will do it step-by-step so you can familiarise yourselves with these locations which will play a role throughout this trial, Gracac, Obrovac, Benkovac, Kistanje, Otric, two towns completely destroyed. We'll talk about that later today. Donji Lapac. And finally Srb, close to the Bosnian border. These areas' mop-up operations were conducted searching the captured areas and small populated villages. Your Honours, turning to map 14, this is an important map. It's an HV military map signed by General Gotovina. It's map 14 in your court booklet. It displays the daily advancement of the Croatian forces from the 4th to the 8th of August. Note the legend in the bottom left-hand corner which shows the original map marking colours. Although the colours, Your Honours, in the legend have faded, it is clear from the coloured arrows that the colour blue, the outer rim, represents the advancing HV forces as of 4th of August. Purple, 5th of August. Green, 6th of August. Orange, 7th of August. And finally yellow, 8th of August. The blue line across the top of the map denotes the northern border of the area of responsibility of the Split Military District during Operation Storm. In the initial phases of the operation, the Special Police commanded by the Accused Markac operated predominantly in the area above that blue line. As the operation progressed, some of the Special Police forces were also deployed below that line and within the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. And I'll show you these locations a little bit later today. The blue dotted line depicts the HV front line, and next to it the red dotted line is the SVK front line, SVK, defending forces. Both together represent the zone of separation. The blue flag-like marks positioned along the HV front line with the dark blue letters depict the HV units at their start positions on 4th August, 1995. And finally on this map at this point, Your Honours, note how the advancing troops, blue, purple, green, orange, yellow, encircle and reduce in size the Serb territory, leaving open an exit for the Serb civilians to flee towards north, their border of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And note that the captured territory, as of 8th of August, which includes all of the areas covered by the coloured arrows. Your Honours, on the 8th of August, General Gotovina reported that the liberation of the whole area within Split Military District so-and-so of responsibility and the tasks assigned to the MD were concluded. Mr. President, Your Honours, as you already heard, by the time Operation Storm was over, the Krajina was in ruins. Hundreds of Serb civilians killed, the remaining Serb population almost entirely gone. Homes, villages, towns looted, destroyed on a massive scale, livestock killed and fields burned. Let me be clear, Your Honours. The loss of life, the killings, the devastation, the harassment of civilians, these crimes were not merely unavoidable, regrettable isolated consequences of warfare, of the operation I have you've just outlined. We will present evidence about the circumstances during which these actions occurred. The evidence will show that these attacks on civilians, their lives, their property, occurred outside the military framework, were not committed in the heat of battle. There was little, if any, defence in the Krajina villages and towns which were devastated by the Croatian forces. There were few, if any, military targets in the civilian populated areas, and the overwhelming majority of people killed were civilians or soldiers hors de combat. In short, there was absolutely no military justification in what the Croatian forces did to the Serb civilians and their property in the Krajina in August 1995. Also, not only are the acts not justified by military necessity, these crimes were not isolated, random acts committed by individual soldiers. You will hear evidence that suggests that the volume, the widespread and systematic nature in which the crimes were committed and indeed the manner in which they were committed openly, with impunity, over a relatively small period of time indicates that the crimes formed part of a campaign. Your Honours, the three accused are charged with nine counts that consists of both crimes against humanity and violations of the laws and customs of war. Charges of persecutions, deportation and forcible transfer, plunder of public and private property, wanton destruction, murder, and finally, inhumane acts and cruel treatment. Your Honours, Mr. Tieger already discussed details of the shelling operation that commenced in the early hours of 4th August, 1995, and that was aimed at and indeed resulted in the expulsion of the Krajina Serbs. Let me focus on what occurred in the heel of the shelling. Immediately after the fall in the afternoon of the 4th of August in Knin, Croatian soldiers began ravaging the town by breaking into homes, shops, and cafes to feast on the bounty of liquor and food left for the taking. At the same time they began looting all of the choice pickings in the town such as abandoned vehicles, televisions, VCRs and even furniture. Not only did they do this all over town of Knin but right in front of the UN compound where they set up a makeshift staging area for the collection of looted items. The UN personnel and Serb refugees who were confined to the UN compound watched helplessly as the Croatian soldiers shot out the locks of vehicles of -- the Serb refugees were forced to leave behind in order to grab whatever might be inside. As the day progressed, 5 August, some Serbs were brought to the UN compound by Croatian soldiers who took photographs and ID cards from the Serbs before taking the keys to their vehicles and driving off with them. When night fell on the 5th of August, small-arms fire could be heard in quick, short bursts as the Croatian soldiers "cleaned the town." They also made sure to continually fire their machine-guns over the UN compound to keep the Serb refugees in a constant state of panic and to intimidate the members of the UN and their local staff. And when I say "cleaned the town," it's inverted commas, of course. A witness will tell Your Honours about a young Serb female who exacted from him a promise to shoot her if the Croats entered the camp because she was afraid of being raped or worse. Such was the fear inspired by the first night of Croat rule in Knin. By the very next day, the burning had already begun. Even with the near total lockdown of all international observers, the Croats could not hide the plumes of smoke rising from towns and villages all over Sector South. Returning to the events in and around Knin on the 5th August. UN military observers, the UNMOs, reported seeing houses burning in Knin. Large plumes of smoke, and we can go back to -- go to map number 31. This is the last map in your booklet, Your Honours. The UNMOs saw plumes of smoke rising from Benkovac. This is approximately 50 kilometres west of Knin. And the entire -- and also the village of Vrbnik, and you can see that about four kilometres south of Knin, marked red with number 6. The entire village of Vrbnik was looted and set on fire. On the said map, 31, in Gracac, this is at the top left marked in green, an UNMO team that made it back into the town observed HV soldiers looting and almost all of the houses partially destroyed. The UNMOs also found five houses as well as their own former accommodation burned to the ground. In Knin, a small number of international personnel managed to make their way into the town where they all witnessed HV soldiers continuing to damage the city in broad daylight in front of and sometimes alongside the military and civilian police. The main street of Knin was being cleansed of the dead bodies and debris which had littered it after the shelling attack and clearing operation the night before. One witness, Your Honours, will describe the two large cattle trucks he saw parked outside the Knin cemetery on this day, and others will describe what appeared to be mass graves being dug in the same area. New windows were being installed on most buildings along the main street, even as others in the town were burning. Fresh paint was being splashed where needed, and shell craters filled in. By the next day all would appear quite undamaged in time for President Tudjman's arrival to the city which would be followed by the international media. In this context, Your Honours, at trial you'll see a video of the Accused Gotovina representing his subordinate commanders for allowing the troops to ravage the town in the face of the imminent arrival of the president. The irony of this situation is inescapable since the very conduct which General Gotovina appears to be complaining about is not only going on right outside the building in which that meeting is taking place but the same conduct continued for weeks and months thereafter. And the Accused Gotovina did little to stop it much less discipline his subordinate commanders who, too, failed to do so. The ingenuity of the Accused Gotovina's apparent fury at the Knin town is reflected in the fact that in the depths of Knin the real aftermath continued to be seen quite clearly. Heaps of debris from shelling and looting damage were piled high and hidden from view of the main street. HV soldiers and police continued to loot the empty houses in Knin with the exception of those marked as Croat houses, which were conspicuously preserved. The Accused Markac also appears on the video. He did equally little to prevent or punish this conduct in the weeks and months that followed. The transcript should reflect the Accused Cermak. I might have misspoken. The Accused Cermak who also appears on the video did equally little to prevent or punish this conduct. And even on the day the video was made, President Tudjman appointed him the military governor for the former Sector South. Nevertheless, despite these pronouncements and orchestrated media events, the realities that the military authorities, members of the HV including military and Special Police not only continued to exercise authority in the southern part of the Krajina but continued to plunder, burn, and murder their way across the countryside ensuring that no Serb would return. Your Honours, one international witness will give you insight into the motives of the perpetrators on the ground. The HV soldiers complained to him that the looting was their reward for participating in the operation as they were lowly paid and it was considered as part of their wages. They said that their senior commanders had specifically authorised them to help themselves to the goods. When asked about the destruction, the killing of livestock and the poisoning of the wells, they explained that this was to prevent the Serbs from returning. The witness will tell you that you understood exactly what they were saying because he comes from a farming background and to destroy the infrastructure and to destroy the means of a villager's livelihood would ensure that no one could return and live in that particular region. Your Honours, on the 7th of August, Mr. Akashi, the UN special representative of the Secretary-General arrived for a tour of Knin and to discuss with Military Governor Cermak the implementation of the 6th August agreement between the UN and the Croatian government regarding the role of UN authorities in the former Sector South under Croatian rule. A major component of this agreement was the guarantee of total freedom of movement for all UN agencies in order to monitor the human rights situation of the remaining Serbs in the region and to provide humanitarian assistance where needed. Ironically, this discussion was being had while -- held while almost the entire population of international observers and Serb refugees remained confined to the UN camp and other various collection centres throughout Sector South. When Mr. Akashi arrived, he was permitted to have a UN security escort. Some UN personnel used this opportunity to conduct reconnaissance in Knin while others accompanied Mr. Akashi. The looting of the town had been so thorough that when Mr. Akashi asked to see an example of a looted house, one of the UN escorts from whom you will hear told him, pick any house. At this Mr. Akashi simply pointed to a house at random and when they entered to inspect it, true enough it had been totally ransacked and looted. On the 8th of August, the UN and other international personnel were finally allowed outside the UN compound. These were members of UNMO, UNCRO, ECMM, and the newly created human rights action teams or HRATs. They had been charged with observing the conduct of the warring factions on behalf of the international community but were suspiciously prevented from doing so by the Croatian authorities during the crucial days when their watchful eyes were most needed. Your Honours, on most of these occasions such restrictions occurred when plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the areas where the Croatian authorities would not permit the internationals to investigate. Nevertheless, through dogged perseverance and circuitous travels of the main roads, many of these internationals were able to observe and document the campaign of burning, looting and killings which occurred in the aftermath of Operation Storm. The members of the joint criminal enterprise, and particularly the three accused, condoned the above conduct, encouraging the Croatian forces to continue. For example, the accused Mladen Markac and minister of interior at that time Ivan Jarnjak arrived in Donji Lapac. If you look at map number 15, it's approximately 80 kilometres north of Knin. Donji Lapac was completely destroyed by members of the MUP Special Police forces and the accused and Mr. Jarnjak commended the personnel for "a job well done." However, in response to the protests from the international community to cease the conduct, lukewarm attempts were made such as issuing orders prohibiting the conduct. However, absent any concrete steps to enforce the orders or punish the breaches, they merely amounted to window dressings for the benefit of the international community. Regarding the widespread burning and looting which occurred, the most comprehensive documented observations of these crimes comes from the UNMOs who conducted systematic service to record the damage done to villages throughout Sector South as well as to locate, record, and provide humanitarian assistance to the remaining Serb civilian population. The reports generated by these UNMOs, and many of them will be witnesses, during the months after Operation Storm establish that by the 27th of August, at least 1.730 houses in Sector South were found to have been totally destroyed and at least 2.600 were partially destroyed. As the Court will hear from the UNMOs who actually conducted this service, there was a standard criteria for determining whether a house was totally or partially destroyed. Specifically, if the roof or construct of a house had been damaged, it was considered totally destroyed; and if it was looted with broken windows or doors, it was considered partially destroyed. As the UNMOs gained access, further access, in Sector South, the figures continued to climb. And, Your Honours, by 13 September, out of 18.232 houses in 240 villages surveyed, more than 13.600, which is 73 per cent, were destroyed after Operation Storm. Only about 650, this is 5 per cent, had been destroyed prior to Operation Storm. The vast majority, Your Honours, of this destruction was done by that time, mid-September. Nevertheless, there are further UN reports that establish that by 4th of October, the number of totally and partially destroyed houses rose to 16.857 out of 21.744, rising even further to a last accounting in 4th November when 17.270 houses out of 22.213 houses had been totally or partially destroyed. As one of the UN observers from whom you will hear very shortly wrote and I will quote: "As the daily situation reports showed every day, the looting and harassing of the remaining population has not stopped even though the presence of the Croatian police has increased in some areas. The looting has decreased, but not mainly because of the increased Croatian police presence. The reason is simpler. There is nothing left to loot." Your Honours, by way of example, I would like to briefly address the situation in three of the towns which were devastated by the Croatian forces without any justification. The first map using again map 31, the last map in your binder, is the town of Kistanje located about 20 kilometres south-west of Knin. The map -- on your map it's marked in green. Before Operation Storm, Kistanje was an almost exclusively Serb town with hardly any Croat civilians living there. Your Honours, you will hear evidence about how this town was completely torched, destroyed, and looted. The 15th Home Guard Regiment entered the town on 6th August, 1995. One witness who defied the restriction of movement will tell you that the looting and burning started as early as 6th of August. International observers, Your Honours, confirm Kistanje was completely destroyed. By the 14th of August, an UNMO patrol observed that about 90 per cent of Kistanje town had been burned down. ECMM observers reported identical observations. UNCIVPOL report of 14th August said 90 per cent of houses burned down, smoke still rising. To finish on Kistanje as one international wrote and I quote him: "We went through Kistanje. Totally destroyed. Still burning. Nothing there. No people, just soldiers. No animals, nothing, but I've got here a lot of smell, strong smell of bodies." Second map, Your Honours, you have heard of this city before, Gracac. On your map 31 it's about 40 kilometres north-west, marked in green here as well. In Gracac, 85 per cent of the buildings were destroyed, either completely or in part. One witness noticed that Gracac was not only destroyed by burning but also had signs that it was shelled. I quote from his witness statement: "This is the first time that it was obvious that they were a target, because there were artillery holes in the ground leading to Gracac, a lot of them. So it was obviously shelled. We didn't see that because we didn't see that, for example, in Kistanje. So they used artillery on it. And if they were like the rest of them, you'd also see rockets. To my knowledge, there was nothing in Gracac of military value. It's just a town, another town with the same houses with red roofs. They got it basically destroyed, just like Kistanje destroyed."
