Here are a few pictures taken by a journalist who will appear before you, Your Honours, on the 8th of August at around the time that the Special Police were moving in the area. First one shows a house burning on the road leading to Gracac. Your Honours, when internationals would note that houses were burned to the ground or completely torched or destroyed, the next photo will show what they meant. This is also taken along the same road as the previous picture. On the same day, members of the Special Police were also seen looting. Here's a Special Police member hot-wiring what appears to be a civilian vehicle and then proudly driving off with it, as you can see on the next picture. And the last photo is a member of a Special Police loading a TV into a truck. Gracac, Your Honours, was also the place of one of the cemeteries where Serbs were buried, although access was refused to internationals for a long time, noting fresh graves on a regular basis. At one point the internationals counted up to 81 crosses with only 10 of them bearing any names. A number of victims that are relevant to this case, Your Honours, were exhumed from this cemetery in Gracac. Last city -- or, rather, village, town, Otric, Your Honours. You'll hear a lot about Otric in this case. On map 13 again, you can see it. It's located about 27 kilometres north-west of Knin. It's located on the way, on the route from Knin to Srb, which was the road taken by most of the civilians when they fled the area. Otric, Your Honours, was completely destroyed. Again, it was a town predominantly inhabited by Serbs. Internationals stated that -- stated the following about Otric in the weeks following the attack: 11th of August ECMM reports: "Every house in Otric had been destroyed by fire." A few days later, 13th August, one of these HRAT teams, human rights group, reported that Otric, among other towns, had been made "virtually unlivable by actions which occurred after the fighting and that the authorities continue to take no actions." You will hear from a witness who will testify that when she went to Otric on the 16th of August "it had been completely burned down." And that "not a single house was left undamaged." I would like to add, Mr. President, Your Honours, that there are a number of HV military documents, HV Croatian forces, military forces documents which make reference to these crimes to illustrate with only two. First one, a report by the Split military command organ for political affairs on the 6th of August. He describes -- the author describes the treatment of property by the Split military personnel, Split Military District personnel immediately upon entering Knin as catastrophic, or the operational diary of the Split Military District notes that on the 11th of August that in relation to Otric, we just talked about that, a quote: "Everything in Otric is burnt down." Killings. Your Honours, let me turn to the civilians who were killed during Operation Storm. The Croatian forces entering the towns and villages on the heels of the shelling anticipated that most civilians to have left by then. As such, when civilians who had still remained there were discovered, they were captured and intimidated, forcing them to leave. Some were threatened with physical force, weapons, and firearms and ordered to leave, while others were fired at, wounded or killed. Croatian soldiers entering the civilian habitat moved from house to house and ordered the frightened civilians out and marched them or forcibly transported them out of these hamlets or villages. Those captured were transferred to collection centres or detained with the objective of preventing them from returning to their settlements. Some who had taken shelter elsewhere and attempted to return to their houses were assaulted and intimidated. Civilians who refused to leave were killed by members of the HV and Special Police forces while relatives and neighbours watched. The perpetrators sometimes publicly announced their crimes for the remaining civilians to hear, knowing that that would influence them to leave -- to flee, induce them to flee. HV soldiers and members of the Special Police forces entering towns fired at civilians and set fire to civilian property, at times burning the inhabitants alive. They entered dwellings of old people who had stayed due to their inability to leave and harassed them, stealing their food and livestock, destroying any possibility for them to remain. Your Honours, the Prosecution will show that over 350 civilians were killed from 4th August to 30th September, 1995, in the relevant Sector South area. From these killings the Prosecution has, as you know, selected eight killings. We call them scheduled killings, where the Prosecution will show that 29 Serb civilians were killed unlawfully. In your court binder, Your Honours, again you will find the locations of these eight scheduled killings on the last map, map number 31. Let me discuss three of these scheduled killings in a little bit more detail. The first example, Mr. President, Your Honours, is killing number 2, which took place in the Plavno valley, a valley that was particularly hard hit by Operation Storm. The location of this incident is marked number 2. The Plavno village essentially consists of a number of hamlets. One of these hamlets is Djurici. The evidence will show that in the morning of the 5th or 6th August, a few shells fell into this isolated hamlet and damaged houses. Seven or eight civilians sought refuge in the cellar of the house of Sava Djuric. Sava Djuric, who was 53 years old at the time and physically disabled, stayed upstairs in the house with his mother. In the afternoon, a Croatian tank entered this hamlet. The Croatian soldiers were wearing camouflage uniforms and black masks. They started burning the houses. A resident from whom you will hear in due course asked a soldier why they were burning her house. The soldier responded that the Serbs had burned Kijevo in the past, so now they were burning this Serb hamlet. Your Honours, Kijevo is about 25 kilometres away from Djurici. But the soldiers did not stop at burning Djurici. They went into the house of Sava Djuric and forced him and his mother out of it. One of the soldiers took the 82-year-old mother down the road while the others threw the invalid, Savo Djuric, in a burning workshop behind the house in the yard. The remains of the house and the workshop can still be seen today. This picture is the location where the workshop was and where the remains of Sava Djuric were found. The next scheduled killing, Your Honours, is the one of Grubori. It indicates that these killings were not only committed by soldiers of the Croatian army but also the Special Police. Again it occurred in the Plavno valley and you see the red number 4 next to it. Members of the Special Police carried out what is now known as the Grubori massacre. One of the civilians, victim to this massacre, was 90 years old. In total, five people were killed. A UN camera, Mr. President and Your Honours, was in the area that day so let me just play a very short clip, it's less than two minutes, about what happened.

Yes, then I understand it. So you were talking about scheduled killings. Please proceed and play the video. You have provided the booth with the hard copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "EJF: We visited the Plavno valley yesterday to meet with the group of residents in one town there and we observed that across the valley another town was apparently on fire, there was a huge plume of smoke. So we visited that town in the afternoon and we found that in fact almost every structure in this hillside village was in flames. "RH: The villagers said they had been called away to a meeting in a nearby village. That meeting never took place. "DG: We waited at the school and no one came. When we looked up here we saw that everything was on fire. We rushed back. There is no one here now. There's no sign of those who stayed behind. Whether they burned or ran away, we don't know. My husband's missing. He may have been burnt. Granny's missing. She may have been burned? She's very old and couldn't run away. "RH: When the fire finally died down, Dusanka and her neighbour were able to search the houses. Later, she showed the UN Human Rights Team where they have found their husbands. "DG: Here, let me show you. That woman was not here. Her husband was ill. He was lying in bed over there. When we came we found him dead. That's all I can tell you. He couldn't hear anything. He was deaf. Look, you see? He's been shot, shot in the head."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours, you will hear detailed evidence about this killing. We also show you the numerous attempts to cover up what happened in Grubori, including by the Accused Cermak and Markac. The third example of a scheduled killing is killing number 7. It's again shown on your map. It has the number 7 attached to it south of Knin. Let me just show you a few pictures so you can get the sense of the place. This one shows you the road on the right side, the main road to Knin leading to the background of the photo. On the right side, parts of it is the gips or plaster factory of Knin. On the left side, you see the Sare hamlet. That is part of the wider Uzdolje settlement. Uzdolje gives its name to the scheduled incident. Now, bearing in mind, Your Honours, this picture was taken last year, so most of these houses you see have been rebuilt in the meantime. We will show you during the course of the trial video footage taken in 1997, which shows most of the houses destroyed. Elements of the 142nd Home Guards Regiment entered this area on the 6th of August as they advanced to meet up with elements of the 7th Guards Brigade coming from south of Knin. If we can go to the next picture, Your Honours. When the Croatian soldiers entered the Sare hamlet which you can see now on the right side, on the morning the 6th of August there were approximately 10 civilians in the hamlet. The soldiers gathered the civilians with the exception of one civilian who was able to run away and hide in the woods, and one elderly and immobile woman was left in her house. These eight civilians, Mr. President, Your Honours, were lined up and summarily executed by one of these soldiers who described himself as an Ustasha to them. This happened just by these large trees to the right of the orange house in the middle of the photo. Seven of the civilians died while the survivor, who sustained injuries to the head and thigh, was able to escape. The houses in the village were burned, including the house with the old invalid woman still inside. Her family later came and gathered her bones. Mr. President, Your Honours, to finish I would like to illustrate the numbers and facts given using four maps. For the purpose of this presentation, we have marked the location and the extent of the crimes perpetrated across the territory on sequential maps. Prior to presenting these maps to you, I would like to first explain the source of the map we will use in this presentation. The first map before you, Mr. President, Your Honours, is a map we have compiled from four different source maps. The basic map covering most of the area is the map you have seen earlier. It's number 14 in your booklet, the map signed by the accused General Gotovina. This map did not extend far enough north to include the area of operation of the Special Police under the command of Mladen Markac, so we have overlaid two maps depicting Special Police movements in the northern area of the map. In order to complete the map, we have incorporated a portion of an UNPROFOR map in the north-eastern corner and the north-western area to ensure that the entire area is depicted. We have produced this compilation map for the reason that the two fundamental maps show the areas that the Croatian army and the Special Police had taken over and controlled at the time the crimes were perpetrated. The second map, Your Honours, includes the incidents of killings, wanton destruction, and plunder for the period 4th of August to 30th of September, 1995. The legend in the top left corner explains the symbols. Yellow for killing incidents, black/orange for wanton destruction, and red/black for plunder. In addition, we have marked with black dots, small black dots, evidence of the presence of the Special Police. As I explained before, Your Honours, as the operation went ahead, the Special Police moved into the area of responsibility of the Split Military District from up north. They moved south. The third map, Your Honours, covers the same information, but in addition we have now overlaid it with the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. Your Honours, there is no better way for you to show and see the widespread and systematic nature of these crimes that were committed by the Croatian forces in the course and in the aftermath of Operation Storm within a relatively small area and during a short period of time. Please be aware, Your Honours, each of these symbols represents atrocious crimes, the loss of lives, and the loss of homes. In short, they represent the shattering of a community and a people. The fourth and last map, Your Honours, represents only the killings, but we added the number of victims killed in each of these locations. Perhaps it can be enlarged a little bit. And I repeat, and by this I end, Mr. President, Your Honours, that we counted only civilian victims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I said before the break page 35, line 13, that I appreciate that, as it appears on the transcript, "formal relationships between those who are assisting us and Defence counsel," of course I meant "informal relationships," that is good working relationships. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, you've now heard that the destruction of the Serb community began with the arrival of the Croatian army and Special Police in the area and continued for weeks. Earlier I cited the anguished comment of an international, "This is criminal. Is there nothing that can be done?" There was much that could have been done but was not, because those in a position of responsibility, indeed those required by law to do so, did not despite their awareness that both the risks that the crimes would occur and the knowledge that they were ongoing and would continue. I know the Court is well aware of the responsibilities incumbent upon superiors, so I don't wish to dwell on that except to briefly touch on a few points. Of course the law requires a commander to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent and punish over those for whom he has effective control, that is the material ability to prevent and punish. And these are two distinct duties. They are not discharged just in the face of generalised orders or cautioning subordinates to act in a lawful manner when particular circumstances arise that render that general responsibility insufficient. The duty to act for a commander exists when he knows or has reason to know that crimes are about to occur, but that does not mean he has to have specific details about a crime which is about to unfold or about which has happened. A commander is required to act when he has general information about unlawful acts that are about to occur or have occurred and the need for measures to be taken. For example, this Tribunal has stated that a commander who has received information that some of his subordinates have a violent or unstable character or have been drinking prior to a mission is considered to have the requisite knowledge and must act. And furthermore, a commander cannot refrain from using the means to obtain such information and then later uses an excuse the fact that he didn't possess it. As the Court will hear, Your Honours, the three accused had ample reason to know both before the operation of the substantial risk that crimes would occur and after the operation that they were occurring, and they failed to act or simply reiterated generalised reminders, the same reminders that had already been proven to be inadequate. And having failed to prevent, they also failed to discipline or punish, thereby progressively undercutting the potential deterrent impact of any sanctions, again in a cycle. With a considerable array of enforcement mechanisms at their disposal, none were meaningfully used, and the results can be seen in a number of ways. The activity reports of the military police, criminal police, for August 1995 reflects a level of activity for the military police covering the Split Military District basically comparable to the month before and basically comparable to the August of the year before. In other words, as if the vast wide-spread crimes of August 1995 simply hadn't happened. You will see similar figures for the military and criminal justice systems with almost no investigations initiated in August and early September. And the disciplinary figures for the Split Military District reveal roughly the same thing, no military disciplinary proceedings of any statistical significance and certainly not for the substantial crimes that occurred, recognising that the disciplinary system is not the primary means of enforcement, but the picture is clear. Little was happening, and to understand the gap between that little that was happening, it's useful to turn now to what the accused knew at the time and what they were doing. Some of this discussion will overlap and be interwoven between accused, but I'll try to take them quickly one at a time. General Gotovina, as you've heard, was the commander of the Split Military District throughout the indictment period. That was the district that clearly functioned on a strict command and control system, a command and control system that General Gotovina himself praised in the book you've already heard about. He had both de jure and de facto control over his troops and the ability to issue orders to the military police. He had constant access to information on the ground, ample mechanisms to ensure that his orders, at least the orders he was interested in were enforced. And although he embarked on other offensive operations during the indictment period, he did not relinquish his command and responsibilities and continued to issue orders even when physically outside the area and remained responsible for the conduct of his troops. Shortly after the operation on August 9th, he ordered the reorganisation of his four operational groups into three operational groups and units from those formations were required to ensure the security and conduct clean-up operations throughout the territory as well as protecting the border and preparing for operations in the east. And you'll also hear testimony that many, many, many troops remained in the Split Military District engaged in the crimes about which you've heard. Moreover, the evidence will show that General Gotovina was often physically present in the indictment area during the months of August and September, spending considerable time in Knin but also in Zadar. It would have been impossible not to observe for himself the crimes that were occurring around him. Now, General Gotovina, like others, knew of the risk of retribution by his troops before it began and indeed, as you'll hear in a moment, he knew of the propensity of those troops for engaging in crimes. As was mentioned before, there were troops. Many of the troops were from the area returning to the place and perceived source of their suffering and their attitude toward Serbs or Chetniks was all too predictable. Indeed General Gotovina told President Tudjman on 31 July: "The forces heading towards Knin are 400 good infantrymen from the 3rd Battalion, the 126th Regiment who are all from this area and they know the area through and through. They have reason to fight here and at this moment it is difficult to keep them on a leash." Indeed General Gotovina would later explain to one of the internationals that this human feeling to hate an enemy who has burned, looted and expelled one's family was in fact an explanation for why the crimes occurred. It was no secret to General Gotovina or to the other commanders in Storm that they were sending in aggrieved men to a place that they saw as the cause of the harm to them and their families. That information alone would have been more than sufficient to trigger some -- something more than boilerplate or customary standard admonitions to abide by the Geneva Conventions or international humanitarian law, but there's more than that, because just a few days before in the prior operation, General Gotovina's troops had committed the same crimes they were to go on to commit during Operation Storm. Let me show you -- I'll read from an excerpt of a report on 13 August from the military police: "On the following day, members of the Croatian army 4th Guards Brigade and the 7th Guards Brigade as well as certain groups ... that came into the broad area of Grahovo from surrounding areas began setting fire to houses in Grahovo and the surrounding villages in an organised fashion." Now, this activity was also reflected in the Split Military District diary which mentioned on July 29th that the entire Grahovo was on fire. So knowing that he was sending in armed men to a place in which they would be quite prone and predisposed to revenge and knowing further of the propensity for committing crimes against Serbs, the measures, both reasonable and necessary, for General Gotovina to have taken extended well-beyond customary instructions concerning compliance. Strong and very specific measures were required such as immediate investigations, detention, dismissal, arrest. It was not only sensible but clearly needed, yet General Gotovina took none of these measures, limiting himself repeatedly as these crimes went on to standard reminders such as instructing units on their obligations or generalised admonitions to prevent looting and burning. And of course what happened after he sent in those troops was all too predictable. You've already heard that the looting and burning commenced right away and you've already heard that General Gotovina knew about it as evidenced by the meeting on August 6th and the video during which he complained about the fact that dignitaries and the media were about to arrive and things were a mess and during the course of which he characterised his troops alternately as barbarians or spoiled children but no orders to deal with those "barbarians" were issued. And again predictably under those circumstances the crimes continued and again General Gotovina had ample reason to know and did in fact know that this was taking place. First of all as Mr. Waespi indicated, these crimes were happening routinely, and the evidence of what was happening was available for everybody. An interesting quote from a witness who wrote: "The ferocity and thoroughness of this senseless destruction is reminiscent of a medieval exorcism of Serbian spirits from the timbers of every building and barn. No village was spared." And as you'll hear from the witnesses, the knowledge about what was happening was available for anyone who cared to look. There are ample excerpts from the Split Military District operational diary indicating those crimes on a chronological and ongoing basis. You heard one from Mr. Waespi. Let me cite just a couple of more. On the 10th: "Everything is looted. The looting is the problem." On the 14th: "The burning of houses and the killing of cattle is being continued." On the 19th: "The problem is the 6th Home Guard Regiment that is burning down the houses in Rasanovci." And then you extend beyond the Split Military District diary operations. Here's an example from a report by the political administration coordinator for the Split Military District on August 13th: "It should be noted that the largest number of fires occurred a day or two following the entry of HV units, that is Croatian army units, into newly liberated villages. Cases of arson were most often carried out by members of Home Guard regiments who were displaced persons from the areas recently liberated. It should be assumed that their motive is revenge." Your Honours, the -- apart from the obvious evidence visible to everyone in the area, it was equally clear that everyone in the military structure knew that these crimes were taking place and were ongoing. And again as I said, as those crimes continued General Gotovina took no steps beyond the generalised prohibitions that I mentioned. On the 10th of August he issued an order to two of the four operational groups to implement military discipline and order, prevent arson and illegal acts and to take resolute measures against those who conduct themselves in an undisciplined manner. That's essentially a reiteration of the duties that were obviously incumbent upon those commanders and upon those troops since before the operation began and had been persistently ignored on an ongoing basis. But perhaps General Gotovina's most telling reaction to the crimes occurred about a week later. Aware again of the ongoing crimes and the inadequacy of his previous responses to it, he noted once more that burning buildings was forbidden and the issue should be resolved. And as for concrete steps, he said this: "The units that are burning down the houses will stay during the winter in the houses they are burning down now." In short, they'll just have to live with the mess they made. A commander has the obligation to take steps to ensure that his orders are carried out or they mean nothing. Indeed if they are not carried out, they mean less than nothing. They become quickly sanctioned and they become a signal to the troops that such behaviour that is supposed to be prohibited is tolerated. And the duty to act is particularly significant when an entire community is being destroyed virtually systematically and over a protracted period of time. Now, Mr. Waespi spoke about killings and the number of Serbian civilians who were killed during the course of the destruction of their community, but it would not be until international pressures mounted weeks later that these later -- that inquiries started to be made for these later victims. The notice began much earlier. Of course it begins with the knowledge of the troops who were going in and the area they're going into. As General Cermak said to President Tudjman, explaining what happened: "You had fighters on the front line for three, four years. They lost their houses, ancestors, land, et cetera. They were already a bid damaged by the Vietnam syndrome and in that state they were killing." It took no stretch of imagination to realise the considerable risk of retribution of that type in the absence of concrete measures to suppress it. And after the operation began there was information from observations of internationals and complaints of internationals, both direct and through the media, that killings were taking place. One interesting one is the report by a UN press officer named Alun Roberts on September 1st when he said, "We basically got a body count of people since the 4th and 5th of August. There's now --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "There's now somewhere near 100 or more." Now, apart from the evidence that you'll hear of the intense interest on the part of Croatian military and political authorities about the possibility of media exposure and their awareness of what the media was saying, the accused were particularly interested in -- and attuned to Mr. Roberts' reports. So as you'll hear, in early September General Gotovina, in a meeting with the UNCRO sector commander threatened to have Roberts executed as a spy and provocateur and General Cermak similarly singled Roberts out in a newspaper article as one who had been writing about Croatia negatively from the very start. But Generals Gotovina and Cermak and General Markac did not need the media to know that Serb civilians were being killed on a large scale. On the 19th of August, General Cermak met with a fact-finding team from the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights and they confronted him with information about summary executions and his response was: "That there are probably --" and I'm quoting from the report. "That there are probably 200 to 300 bodies in the hills with bullet holes in their heads." When they pressed him for more information, nothing was forthcoming. But these accused did not need the media to know that Serb civilians were being killed. Those bodies weren't secreted away only to be discovered years later to everyone's surprise. They were officially collected and counted on a daily basis, and Generals Gotovina and Cermak and Markac knew that because they used or established the very sanitation groups that were out there collecting the bodies. General Cermak did that immediately when he arrived in Knin, and General Gotovina did that on August 11th. Now, General Gotovina's order for attack had anticipated that such a detachment would work with the civilian police and they did. So as the sanitation units prepared reports daily, the -- they provided them to -- they provided that information to the police and the chief of the Zadar crime police, who was -- that was one of the police administrations involved in General Gotovina' order, reported on the progress of sanitation operations. And General Cermak was regularly apprised about the bodies collected. Let me show you an example of one of the reports by the chief of the Zadar crime police setting out the details of the corpses collected by the 9th of August. This is the type of information that was available about the number of civilians being killed. And you've heard the final statistics. Over 350, and I believe the evidence will show even more were killed, and that is civilians, during August and September, during the indictment period. Now, the Defence in its pre-trial brief has asserted that General Gotovina essentially relied upon, was informed that the civilian and military police and authorities were taking effective action and were restoring order and discipline in the liberated areas. Well, first, a commander cannot evade his fundamental responsibility to control his troops by pointing at others who may have been in a position to do so after they committed crimes. The responsibility to control those troops lies first and foremost with the commander, and the reason is, as you'll hear, that if he fails to do so, there is little that can be done in response. In any event, General Gotovina knew full well that the civilian and military authorities were not -- military police authorities were not coping with the crimes. The evidence of that failure and the evidence of what his troops were doing was before his eyes at any given moment. But let me address the activities of the civilian military police authorities quickly, perhaps too quickly, in any event. First of all, everybody knew that the civilian authorities would take time to get established and functional. As President Tudjman said, the military may not be able to do all the things civilian authorities ultimately can, but "they can maintain order in these transitional periods." General Gotovina knew this. He told internationals in a meeting on August 8th that the military governor would remain in Knin until civilian authority was established. General Cermak was there until November. It was also clear that the civilian authorities were not going to be able to cope with the extensive crimes committed by soldiers at that time. There was never a genuine prospect of that happening. They weren't really set up to do that. They didn't have the real clout and authority to. Indeed the civilian police in the area answered to General Cermak and were implementing his orders. Furthermore, the Serb commanders in the area, and there were Serb commanders there pursuant to a constitutional provision regarding the old ethnic demographics weren't really in charge. They answered to people in -- who actually wielded power in Zadar and Zagreb, and as I said, to General Cermak. The -- but perhaps more importantly and understandably, the civilian police, vastly outnumbered by the military, were extremely wary of interfering with armed and marauding soldiers. And you'll see a number of reports indicating that and I'll quote quickly from two. After reporting that members of the HV had been torching houses and killing livestock, the chief of the Lika Sinj police administration writes: "In conversations with individual officers, they have stated that they are powerless with regard to this problem." And similarly, the assistant minister for the police wrote: "It is apparent that houses are being burned down and other people's property is being stolen on a daily basis." He writes: "The perpetrators of those acts in most cases are formally and in effect members of the Croatian army, although there are some persons who are not and are abusing the HV uniform. I hope you will understand that the civilian police faces -- the problem the civilian police faces 'the fact that the perpetrators wear HV uniforms completely blocks the work of the civilian police.'" Now, that would have rendered the civilian police and their efforts inadequate enough, but in fact the limited resources they had were not devoted to protecting Serbs but, in fact, to collecting and interrogating them. That was pursuant to something called Operation Povartak or Return, the priorities of which were to collect suspected prisoners of war, basically meaning anyone of military age, any male of military age, collect civilians in reception centres purportedly for their protection, and sanitize bodies killed during the operations and afterwards, in the aftermath. The diversion of police resources to this task was not a secret and no surprise. It was anticipated before the operation was launched and can be found in General Gotovina's order for attack. In short, the efforts or the lack of efforts by the civilian police contributed to the reign of impunity that existed for perpetrators of crimes against Serbs during this period and that de facto impunity actually became official on August 18th for those who had committed crimes up to that point. And I'm going to read from an encoded order from the assistant minister of the interior to the police administrations. First he recounts the houses that are torched and burned, again indicates that these individuals -- that most of those acts are perpetrated by Croatian army members, notes that the destruction is assuming such proportions that it is inflicting political damage to the Republic of Croatia, and then notes that the local police administration chiefs must immediately convene a meeting with the commanders of military police battalions to inform them of the problem. And so now that damage to Croatia is happening, something should be done. And then: "The meeting must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today." Thus the civilian and military police were instructed not to investigate or operatively process the crimes that had taken place. Now, by that time much of the Krajina was in flames. A huge amount of Serb property had been looted and stolen and many had been killed. The impunity bestowed by this order is not only a further reflection of the negligible impact of the police but sent a continuing signal along with the absence of any meaningful measures from the military commanders that crimes against Serbs were tolerated. The commanders didn't act. The civilian police didn't act, and I'll turn to the military police in a moment. Nobody acted to stop the crimes. Now, General Gotovina does point to the military police, as I mentioned, and cites his reliance on the military police. There are three reasons why no commander can reasonably fail to act on that basis. First of all, as I mentioned, a commander has the responsibility to command and control his troops. That responsibility ultimately rests with him, not with others. Second, he knew that the military police were not investigating crimes. And third, in any event, the military police was a body under his daily operational control. With respect to the first that a commander is the principal figure responsible for his troops and that if he fails to control them there is no realistic prospect that the back-up mechanisms to respond to their crimes will cope, I'll quote as an illustration a report from a high-ranking military police official making precisely that point on August 3rd. After stating the tasks of the military and civilian police he said referring to a meeting the previous day with high-level officials, including General Gotovina: "It had been pointed out to the commanders of the HV units that they were personally responsible for the discipline of their subordinates as without that even a much greater number of military police members could not maintain discipline." As for awareness that the military police were not coping with the problem and that a commander needed to do something, apart from the visible extent of crimes before him General Gotovina was specifically informed that that was the case. He was -- this is a portion of a report addressed to commanders of military districts including General Gotovina on August 17th, again reporting that houses are being torched, property is being looted and other unlawful actions by Croatian army soldiers and civilians wearing HV uniforms are occurring on a daily basis. The communication also says that cooperation between the military police and civilian police on liberated territory thus far has not yielded results. And finally, the third element of any suggestion that General Gotovina could excuse his inaction by pointing to the military police, in fact by pointing to the military police General Gotovina is inadvertently pointing to himself because the military police were subordinated to him for the -- and he had daily operational control. I won't go into details about this, but essentially the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police provide that the military police administration has a -- their own hierarchy and supervisory control over the military police. That's a kind of vertical control. But it specifically provides in Article 9 of those rules that military district commanders have daily operational control, and that's a kind of vertical control, to ensure that the people on the ground are in a position to direct the military police to the very place they're needed at the very time. And you'll see an order in connection with Storm issued by the head of the military police which relates that in the command of daily operations military police battalion commanders shall be subordinated to the Croatian army military district commanders. In short, Your Honours, having brought in the very same troops who had just committed crimes into an area where they were even more likely to do it, General Gotovina did nothing more than issue perfunctory orders to his subordinates reminding them of their obligations, the very obligations they had ignored before and they were ignoring over and over again. Under those circumstances in the climate of ongoing daily widespread crimes, his failure to take those measures not only was a failure to discharge his responsibility but sent a message of toleration and acquiescence to his troops making the continuation of those crimes inevitable and leading to those troops who told the international that Mr. Waespi referred to that their commanders thought it was just fine. But, Your Honours, General Gotovina was not the only General, not the only Colonel-General, indeed, in the area. General Markac was also there, an associate of President Tudjman who was a long-standing member of the HDZ and both a political and military figure. General Cermak did not participate in the planning of Operation Storm or its commencement, but on August 5th he was formally appointed directly and personally by President Tudjman as the Knin Garrison commander and sent there in President Tudjman's own words for the purpose of keeping order. Now, beyond General Cermak's de jure powers as garrison commander which is a position in the military that exists for the purpose of discipline, he was also vested with his authority of his high rank, colonel-general, and the considerable authority emanating from being a personal emissary of President Tudjman for the very purpose of taking charge. Indeed General Cermak was understood by internationals to be the military governor of the area and that was a term used by them throughout in their dealings with them that appears in correspondence and that was not corrected by him. Everyone accepted the appellation of military governor in connection with General Cermak's duties. He was not an operational commander and his presence there didn't interfere with General Gotovina's control over his troops, but by virtue of his position as garrison commander and his even broader de facto authority arising from the factors I've just described, General Cermak possessed effective control and the material ability to discipline and punish Croatian army soldiers within the garrison area. Indeed in the course of his military governor tasks, he used -- he issued orders for activity or coordinated in operations that extended beyond the garrison area. He was able to direct the military and civilian police, as you'll hear, and he had the responsibility and power to punish and, by so doing, prevent crimes against Serbs. Instead, as you'll hear, he exercised his power principally to ensure that Croatia's public image was not damaged with the international community, even when that meant ignoring, excusing, or even covering up crimes against Serbs. Now, General Cermak has asserted that he did not function in a military role. He has characterised himself instead as something like the Red Cross. A man with no authority who was garrison commander only so he could take advantage of logistics and was in Knin to restore electricity and open the water and liaise with the international community. And he's further said that while he was appalled at the crimes that were taking place and repeatedly pleaded with others to do something about it, because he wasn't really a military figure he was not the person responsible in any way for addressing them. In that sense, like General Gotovina, he points to others as failing to do a job for which he was responsible. But the evidence will show, Your Honour, that General Cermak was a military figure, as I've said, with the authority to order the military police and the power as -- as the effective military governor to order the civilian police. He knew that crimes against the Serbian community were being committed by the army. He knew that nothing effective was being done about it, and instead he used his role as described to deflect international pressure and cover up crimes. Let me address those in order. First, General Cermak was unmistakably a military figure. He was mobilised from the reserves. He had the rank of colonel-general. He wore a uniform. He himself acknowledged in the course of recorded interviews with the OTP that he was responsible under military discipline had he done something wrong. Now, his military position was also reflected in other ways. For example, his involvement in mopping up operations. And this series of correspondence that you'll see during the course of the case will reflect that. First on August 21st, the Croatian army chief of staff issued an order for mop-up operations which said responsible for the realisation of this order are the commanders of the military districts as well as the commander of the Knin Garrison. And when General Markac reported to the chief of staff the next day he noted that: "At 1200 hours there was a short meeting with Generals Gotovina and Cermak." And on the 25th, General Cermak responded to the order of the 21st noting that in respect to part of the order that called for an intelligence assessment: "The Split Military District command and Knin Garrison are in constant coordination. The intelligence assessment regarding this order was made by the chief of the intelligence department of Split Military District command. If we were to submit the same, I would consider it a repetition of work." He was clearly a military figure and the evidence will further show that he had the power to issue orders as colonel general to the military police and the power as the effective military governor, emissary from President Tudjman to issue orders to the civilian police who understood they were to implement those records. First I'd like to show you an order to the commander of the Knin military police and the commander of the Knin police station to form teams to find material and return property misappropriated from UNCRO and report back to him. "This order enters into force immediately," as the order says. And here's one on August 8th. Also to the military and civilian police, also effective immediately. You'll also hear witness testimony that General Cermak held daily meetings with the military and civilian police who, as I mentioned before, understood that the conclusions from those meetings were to be implemented. And as he has acknowledged himself in the course of the interviews I mentioned: "I got reports from the military police." He also acknowledged this power contemporaneously at the time, telling members of the international community that he would order or that he had ordered investigations of the crimes they reported. On August 24th, when internationals again raised the issue of continuing crimes, he said he had already issued strict orders to the civilian and military personnel to stop such acts. And again on September 3rd, he responded to UNCRO Commander Forand concerning restriction of movement, telling him that he, General Cermak, had issued a "strict order that it be investigated." Similarly he described in one of his interviews his reaction when he learned that humanitarian aid that he had delivered had been stolen. He was furious he said, immediately called the police commander and told him "do whatever you want. I want the culprits found." And indeed they were. Now, I said that General Cermak was a military figure who had the power to do something about these crimes and he knew about these crimes and knew that crimes were being committed by the army. First he knew about it from the internationals who repeatedly brought it to his attention. You will hear from those internationals and you'll see contemporaneous reports, but as General Cermak himself told OTP representatives about the complaints: "This was a daily problem. It was a constant problem. It was a problem that just went on." Now, beyond his awareness from the reports and protests of the international community, General Cermak himself has repeatedly acknowledged during the course of those interviews with the OTP that he knew that soldiers were committing crimes during that period. "Most of the military wasn't -- wasn't conducting themselves the way they should have." "So when we talk about torching and destruction that was in the first week of the Croatian military going through. So that was one period. And then after that this also happened but to lesser degree; so we have two periods." Here's another quote: "You know that there were some killings, there was looting and burning also after the operation of the Croatian military, and that went on." General Cermak also recounted a telephone conversation with the head of the political affairs administration of the Ministry of Defence. Now, this happened after General Cermak read a newspaper interview in which the head of the political affairs administration had denied that the Croatian army was committing crimes and attributed those crimes to civilians dressed in military uniform, which General Cermak knew was not true so he, according to him, called the head of political affairs on the phone and said: "You idiot. What are you saying? You think these people have no eyes to see what was going on? You're sitting there in Zagreb. You don't even know what the situation is, and the truth is what I'm telling you now." Interestingly, according to General Cermak, the head of political affairs said: "Well, don't be upset with me. You know I don't think like that. There are people higher up." Knowing that these crimes were taking place, General Cermak also knew that insufficient measures were being taken. Indeed that virtually nothing was being done. Here's what he said about that: "From day-to-day I told them: Do your work. Start doing something. Look what's going on in Knin." He stated: "They were there to do their jobs and they were just hanging around, not knowing what to do with themselves." Those are references to the military and the civilian police. According to General Cermak, he was constantly telling others of the criminality that was occurring in the Krajina and beseeching them to do something. He was in touch, he stated with the Minister of the Interior Ivan Jarnjak and with President Tudjman: "Because I didn't understand that this was happening and we couldn't stop this and I was embarrassed this was happening."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Cermak said that he made repeated appeals for the crimes by the army to be dealt with. "I made appeals to the civilian police, the military police. I went to the office of the president. I even called Mr. Jarnjak. I talked to Mr. Gotovina." And then later he said: "I told him clearly, Ante, the military is doing nasty things. We have to stop that." "All the way to the president because I didn't understand that this was happening and we couldn't stop this and I was embarrassed this was happening." So according to General Cermak, he knew that insufficient measures were being taken to address the crimes that, as he told the political affairs head, any idiot could see. He thus admits that he did not take the measures necessary to stop the crimes because he claims he lacked the power to do so. Instead, he beseeched those who had the power, Jarnjak, Tudjman, Gotovina, to do something. Now, these claims acknowledge the ongoing crimes by the army about which everyone knew but then seek to deny his own power and responsibility to act. But apart from failing to use the power and responsibility he had, General Cermak also worked to ensure that international pressures to stop the crimes were deflected. He repeatedly assured the internationals that all necessary steps were being taken or attempted to mislead them into believing that it was not the army that was committing the crimes. I'll quote from a letter that he sent to the ICRC in response to their complaints about the crimes echoing the very claims that he says he told the head of political affairs were untrue. "Crimes that you are referring to were committed by individuals who want to take advantage of a brilliant military operation to gain property in an illegal manner and fulfil sick murderous instincts. Such individuals are criminals who by putting on camouflage uniforms shed suspicions on the honesty of the Croatian soldier and the correct policies of the Republic of Croatia. The government of the Republic of Croatia has shown firm views and determination that all such criminals be brought to justice." Similarly on the 31st of August, the head of UNCRO Sector South wrote him about the smoke coming from the areas where UNCRO had been restricted and posed the question that these unexplained burnings leave many unanswered questions: How is it that almost after a month so many houses continue to be burned, driving poor and destitute persons homeless from their land? And on September 3rd, General Cermak wrote back: "I am surprised that you mentioned the expulsion of the poor and needy from their land and I consider these to be serious allegations and baseless accusations. Please provide documentation to prove at least one case of expelling people and torching their houses." As General Cermak told President Tudjman in 1999: "He had to oppose incessantly to the Helsinki Watch, the international community, arsons, killings, et cetera." Now, in doing that he was just one part of the effort to ensure that crimes were not inadvertently revealed to the international community. You'll see repeated documents during the course of this case, I've cited a couple before, reflecting concern over international repercussions or the fear of damage to Croatia's image, but the objective to ensure that the international community did not receive information that might hurt Croatia's image was pursued in various ways rather than stopping the crimes themselves. For example, Mr. Waespi told you that the UNCRO personnel was locked down and when they were finally released they observed the efforts that had been made to eliminate evidence of what had happened. There was a similar effort to control journalistic access for fear that the media would expose the ongoing crimes. Now, this began before Storm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At a meeting on August 2nd, the political department of the Split Military District reported that journalists were asking to come to Grahovo which had been burned down by HV troops. The quote was in the diary: "Journalists requesting to come to Grahovo. Do not allow journalists to come to Grahovo. Cameras to be controlled." And then General Gotovina, who knew precisely how the damage to Grahovo had occurred then suggested they disseminate an alternative explanation. "Report through a messenger that Glamoc and Grahovo were shelled by phosphoric shells." After Storm that same concern continued, in fact was amplified and you will see various references to that during the course of the case. I will quote again from the Split Military District war diary. "Burning down of houses is a huge problem. The journalists and others who come to visit the area could prove that it was the arson." And then a later reference to different foreign TV agencies coming and the insufficient number of check-points to control journalists from getting in. General Cermak's efforts, however, to cloak the crimes and prevent their exposure to the international community went beyond the measures already discussed, however. Now, I mentioned earlier the collection of bodies in the absence of investigation, bodies that were simply picked up, tagged, photographed, and buried along with the forensic evidence with them. Civilian bodies, animal carcasses were collected as quickly as possible and basically treated with the same investigative interest. Despite the fact that these civilian deaths mounted, these were considered collateral damage, Storm damage. But it's possible to understand more clearly the attitude toward these deaths by pulling the curtain behind which some of these incidents are cloaked and looking at one in particular. Mr. Waespi mentioned Grubori, and I'd like to focus for a moment on what happened in the aftermath of Grubori. Now, that's the incident in which five people were killed, including the 78-year-old man you saw in the video and a 90-year-old woman with a bullet in her head, burned in her house. So similar events of course had happened before. There was one difference here. The human rights action team was virtually on the spot with a camera, and they forced certain actions and responses that enable us to see both the attitude toward killings of Serbs and General Cermak's view of what to do about them. So let's begin with the day of the operation. First General Markac's Special Police members were involved in the mopping up of Grubori. And during the course of that day through radio contact as they were reporting back, they reported that nothing had happened and when they returned that evening they reported that nothing had happened. But the same day, the human rights action team came in with cameras and entered the village and then confronted General Cermak later on. And if I can show you a quick video of his comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, has a hard copy of the transcript been provided to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] There are still some scattered groups of renegades and terrorists on the ground and our own anti-terrorist units of the civilian police are mopping up the area. In one such clean-up action yesterday, they covered 100 kilometres of land towards the villages of Plavno and Grubor. Our troops are performing their normal tasks. "However, the general denied that civilians had been killed or houses burned. "I don't know where you got the information from that the people were called out from their houses, some were in pyjamas and that houses were burned. I will personally submit an official report on this and I think that your information is not really accurate." In this case, however, under pressure from the internationals, it was clear that saying nothing happened was not going to work. So General Markac and his troops went for the easy justification, combat activity. General Markac obtained backdated reports from, first, the commander of the unit and then later, realising there were no reports from the subcommanders who had actually conducted the operation, obtained backdated reports from them as well. All of these reports say that killings occurred as an unfortunate consequence of combat. And these are interesting reports which the Court will have an opportunity to see. Of particular interest is the fact that at some point someone realised that these reports needed an added touch and so the same reports were redone with an extra paragraph which said that before the operation they had been instructed to comply with international law. That's that last paragraph you see in this document. But there was a small problem and that was the two local civilian police wanted to investigate, but that was quickly dealt with. Both were reprimanded not to initiate an investigation. One was called to General Cermak's office, and there the minister of interior was telephoned by General Markac's assistant commander to complain about what the local police were trying to do and it seemed at that point that the matter was successfully buried. Meanwhile, however, General Cermak was assuring the internationals that the victims had died in combat. So in a letter to the ICRC chief of delegation on August 30th, he assured her that: "The Croatian army has and observed strict rules about the protection of civilians." And emphasised: "I personally visited the area the following day and convinced myself of the truth and course of the incidents in question."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for me to follow, I heard and the transcript reads: "One was called to General Cermak's office and there the minister of interior was telephoned by General Markac's assistant commander --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, in General Markac's presence after a conversation with General Cermak and the assistant to that local civilian police officer pushing him not to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, in General Cermak's office by the assistant of General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just noted General Cermak's comment that he personally visited and convinced himself of the truth. The Court has had an opportunity to see that scene, and perhaps it wasn't visible on the video, but that includes bullet casings on the floor where one of the victims was murdered, which is hardly suggestive of collateral damage until the battle took place in that victims' bedroom. Well, not surprisingly, people realised that none of this made sense and Grubori was referenced in a report by the Special Rapporteur Elizabeth Rehn and this is 7th of November.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event the point was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At least one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and Rehn wrote the Foreign Minister emphasising some of the factors that made this clearly appear to be murder rather than combat. And so General Markac was contacted as a result of this letter and he came up with now the third and most implausible version, his new version was that the victims had been executed as the evidence indicated but by Serb terrorists. Now, this version was so transparent that when the Croatian officials responded to Rehn, they didn't even mention it. And in fact this version was too preposterous for even General Markac to maintain and in 2001 when he was interviewed by Croatian investigators looking into Grubori, he reverted to the original coverup story, that the victims had been killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the exclamation marks we find in the margin, are they put there in the original as well or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have the original, Your Honour. My recollection is that's right but we will check and get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for us to be sure. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So let me quickly recap. The first story is that nothing happened. Then, when the killings couldn't be denied it was said to be result of combat activities, and when that was challenged, then Serb terrorists were responsible. And when that clearly couldn't be sustained, General Markac reverted back to the combat activity story which hadn't made sense in the first place. The true story is that the Special Police murdered the victims and destroyed the village and that together, Generals Markac and Cermak worked to ensure that this would never be known. Now, General Markac's cover-up would have been significant enough if he was simply another superior officer of the Lucko unit which was involved; but as the assistant minister of the interior for Special Police and the commander of the Special Police forces during Storm, he set the standard for every member of that body.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters and I'll write it down on each page. The Special Police was originally designed to be an elite force within the Ministry of the Interior to fight sabotage and combat terrorism, and they were also, as they did in Storm, to participate in combat operations as specialised infantry forces. After combat, they were used to mop up. They were heavily armed with everything from pistols, rifles, machine-guns, to anti-tank rocket launchers, mortars, and multiple-rocket launchers. During and for a time after Operation Storm, Special Police forces were operationally subordinated to the Croatian army with General Markac reporting both to the Croatian army Main Staff and to the minister of the interior. He had mechanisms to receive reports about upcoming, ongoing, and completed operations and had the authority to order investigations and initiate disciplinary actions against subordinates. And despite the obvious crimes that were taking place all around him and that were clearly committed by his men, he chose like his fellow accused not to do anything, not to punish anyone, or, rather, he chose to do the opposite. From the virtual outset of entering towns and villages the Special Police began committing crimes. As Mr. Waespi indicated, they entered Gracac on the 5th and within a short time the town was destroyed or was being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Could you perhaps put it every ten lines, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ultimately, as you have heard, 85 per cent of Gracac was destroyed and you saw those photographs of the Special Police members loading televisions on trucks and hot-wiring cars. General Markac could always know where his men were. He received regular reports, but in Gracac he didn't need to read reports to know that. He was there with them. On the morning of the 5th of August, he entered Gracac with his Special Police and set up his forward command post there at noon. And that's the -- I think you can see that at the arrow. A few days later, on the 7th of August, the Special Police entered Donji Lapac in much the same way as they entered Gracac. As with Gracac, the town was set ablaze and as with Gracac the burning continued for days. Ultimately, Donji Lapac was virtually completely destroyed. As the minister of defence said in September to President Tudjman: "President, Donji Lapac as such does not exist. There is only its name on the map. Everything is destroyed, everything." Here, too, General Markac didn't need to rely on the widespread awareness of the looting and burning or the reporting system that would have alerted that to him -- excuse me, to the presence of his units in the locations where the looting and burning was taking place. He was in Donji Lapac as the evidence will show and he could see it for himself. Now, in light of what you've heard about Grubori, it's no surprise that no disciplinary measures or criminal penalties were imposed against members of the Special Police for crimes. General Markac's interest was not in disciplining his troops, not in preventing these crimes, not in punishing these crimes but in ensuring the opposite, that these crimes would not be brought to light, that they would be buried along with the victims. We talked Grubori already. The very day after the Grubori massacre, on the 26th of August, the same unit involved conducted a mop-up operation in the municipality of Orlic. And you have you've heard from Mr. Waespi what happened to Orlic. In the course of this operation they began setting fires. General Markac was present immediately after the incident. In this case he argued with the subordinate commander who had led the unit over the manner in which the operation was conducted. But he didn't punish, discipline, or arrest the members of the unit despite the fact that he knew that they were the unit which had just set fire -- General Markac was aware that this unit which had just set fire to the village was the same unit involved in Grubori the day before. Instead of the necessary punishment, punishment that would have sent a message that had long since been needed in -- in the face of the ongoing crimes, he simply withdrew them to Zagreb. And then this incident, too, was covered up by General Markac, just like Grubori. In his report to the chief of staff on the Special Police operation for that date, he reported that this fire occurred in the course of combat. And indeed when you have an opportunity to look at those reports you can see the similarities. This false characterisation just like in Grubori served as a means of cloaking crimes by his subordinates, crimes that he was responsible for preventing and punishing, not covering up. Your Honours, the circumstances that I have outlined, the unlawful failures of those with responsibility, the climate of impunity, the cover-ups did not happen by accident. They can be traced back to the objective I described at the beginning of my remarks, to drive Serbs out of the Krajina and keep them out. As discussed, the three accused contributed to that objective in various ways, whether actively or by repeatedly turning a blind eye, by standing by as the destruction unfolded day after day and yet repeatedly failing to take necessary steps to prevent or to stop the crimes. In so doing, as I've said before, the message that was sent is the one that was received by the soldier who talked to that international that Mr. Waespi referred to, who understood that his conduct was tolerated and permissible. It is for these reasons that the indictment charges a joint effort to achieve the illegal objective identified in the indictment. Your Honours, twice earlier I referred to the anguished rhetorical question posed about an international in the midst of the destruction of the Serb community, a community which had resided in that part of the Krajina for centuries: "This is criminal. Is there nothing that can be done?" Well, at this point what can be done now is the trial that we have embarked today which promises a full and fair account of those events with due regard to the rights of the accused and the rights of the victims and to the solemn responsibility to ensure that to the extent possible, the full story of what happened based on all the available evidence will emerge and responsibility allocated accordingly. It is the Prosecution's submission, Your Honours, that at the end of this trial, having heard all the evidence, you will find the accused guilty of the crimes charged in the indictment. This concludes my opening remarks and Mr. Waespi's opening remarks for the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Having finished for today, we'll adjourn unless there's anything to be raised. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did want to say something. I should have addressed it earlier but I didn't want to take time away from the Prosecution's opening statement. We have extensive use of videos in our opening statement tomorrow. We have already sent an instruction to our team to get as many transcripts as possible to the interpreters in the booth but I did want the Trial Chamber to be aware that I'm not positive yet that we're going to have all the transcripts, but we're going to do everything possible to get that done by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you understand my concern for a complete transcript. On reviewing this this afternoon, whether you have all the material available, try to imagine what practical problems could arise on those clips for which you have no hard copy available. If these are longer clips, that might create an unworkable situation. If it's a very short clip, you might read at the appropriate speed something into the transcript. Perhaps also the parties could consider this afternoon to what extent videos played or audios played are later tendered because then there might not be that much of a need to have them all marked for identification. If, however, this is material that will not come at any later stage, then I think it would be wise to have them marked for identification. Perhaps it would even be a good idea that if not every single part would be marked for identification that at least, in one way or the other, it is on the record what has been played, for example, by just providing a short list, finding them, index of video and audio material played during opening statements can be filed then we don't have to pay any attention to it any further, but then the record is at least complete. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, the same courtroom.
